Mr. Vennor the weather-wise Canadian, predicts a wet June, with frequent severe wind and thunder storms, and probable frosts between the fifth and tenth of the month. He says: "The 'north waters' are only coming down now, which is an indication of wet June. The warmest part of June is likely to occur between the twentieth and twenty-fifth when the heat will be excessive."

The grain traffic of the Mississippi last year exceed 25,000,000 bushels. The business is very remunerative, and this season the fleet will be largely increased. It is believed that the season's traffic this year will approach 100,000,000 bushels. The entire movement of grain to the seaboard last year was 230,000,000 bushels. This division of the traffic with railroads East is already making itself felt in the railroad stock market.

In his last letter THE BULLETIN's regular Washington correspondent says: "Our present and prospective relations with Mexico are being made a study by the secretary of state. He sees the probability that difficulties will arise from the vast amount of our capital now being invested in that country, and from the emigration which is just beginning but which promises to become great. While this government is not in any way connected with these movements, and congress wisely ignored the request of Captain Eads to guarantee the bonds for his marine railway across Mexican territory, the secretary knows that we may at any moment be called upon to protect our citizens in Mexico. The turn of affairs is so sudden and unprecedented that the administration in the event of trouble, will have to work out an entirely new course of action." He says further: "Secretary Blaine and Sir Edward Thornton, the British minister, have concluded negotiations by which the British government is bound to pay £15,000 sterling to the United States, to indemnify American fishermen who suffered loss by the Fortune bay outrage."

About eleven o'clock night before last the young negro, who committed the outrage upon Mrs. Kobler, was captured at his home, at the corner of Twenty-ninth and Sycamore streets. Sheriff Hodges, Marshal Myers and Officer John Tyler were engaged in the hunt and it was greatly due to the latter that the fellow was discovered and captured as soon as he was found. The officers had but very little clue to work upon and therefore deserve much credit for making the capture with such dispatch. The young wretche's name is Albert Hayes; he is quite black, weighed about a hundred and fifty pounds and is about nineteen years of age. He has served a term in the state reform school, from which he was discharged about last Christmas. Yesterday in the presence of Sheriff Hodges and Marshal Myers he made a full confession of his crime, which coincides almost entirely with the account published in yesterday's BULLETIN; with the exception that he denies having dragged his victim to the pond by the hair of her head. The wounds about her head, he said, were caused by her fall. His preliminary trial will probably come off to-morrow.

—The failure of the school board to re-elect Prof. G. G. Alvord as superintendent of the Cairo public schools is a matter that is not without some weight. Every important change with respect to the public schools must be a matter of grave public concern, and therefore it is to be hoped that each member of the board pondered will before casting his vote for, or against a change in the office of superintendent of the public schools. That this was done, and that the change was made, solely because it was thought to be to the interest of the public that it should be made, we have no doubt; for the members of the board are all estimable gentlemen who can lay aside all feelings in conflict with the public good when occasion requires. But if there is any ground for the belief that the interests of the Cairo public demand a change of management in the schools, then that ground must be found outside of those schools. For, so far as we know, no change could be made in them that would improve the character either with respect to their management or general reputation. CAIRO, ILL., June 4.—A colored boy named Albert Hayes was lodged in the county jail at midnight, charged with having knocked down and ravished an old German woman named Koehler, above this city last evening. She is seriously injured about the head. He was dragging her by the hair to throw her in a goose pond, when a colored man came by and rescued her.
albert-hayes-1881-06-07.A3:
ATTEMPT AT LYNCHING.
Although during the past few days numerous threats have been heard which did not bode well for the young negro, Albert Hayes, who recently assaulted Mrs. Kobler a short distance above the city, it was generally believed that no effort would be made which would tend to curtail the young rascal's earthly existence. About one o'clock yesterday morning, however, a body of masked men—numbering about forty—gathered at the county jail with the fixed determination of mobbing the negro.

The mob approached the jail very quietly and found no difficulty in gaining an entrance, since the outside doors had been left open on account of the excessive heat. Having reached the hall, where Mike and John Fitzgerald, sons of our coroner, were asleep, they cov-
albert-hayes-1881-06-07.A4: ered the young men with their weapons before they had an opportunity of rising, and demanded the keys of the jail, whereupon Mike, arising from the cot, ran into the kitchen for the apparent purpose of procuring the keys but really for the purpose of giving the alarm. He was however, closely followed and his object becoming apparent, he was surrounded and threatened with instant death unless he procured the keys. At this juncture his brother, John who had also been permitted to leave his bed, put in an appearance with a shotgun and leveling it at the crowd, demanded his brother's release, which demand was complied with. John then escaped from the building and making his way across the street secured the assistance of his father, Mr. Richard Fitzgerald, who, having already heard the noise created by the mob, shortly afterwards put in an appearance. Before his arrival however, the mob had been actively at work making their way to the young criminal. They had already, with a crow-bar and axe, broken open the door by which the hall way leading to the negro's cell is reached and had also destroyed two of the three locks to the cell door which parted them from the object of their search, when Mr. Fitzgerald put in an appearance and demanded that they vacate the building—very emphatically, telling them at the same time that they could not obtain the prisoner without inflicting bodily injury upon him. Mr. Fitzgerald was unarmed, but was perfectly cool and fully determined that the prisoner should not be taken, and by his conduct convinced the mob that they must inflict injury upon him and his sons before their object could be obtained. Upon entering the jail Mr. Fitzgerald had ordered that the fire bells be rung tor assistance, and the clanging of the bells, which now commenced, also probably, had some effect upon the crowd which had already shown signs of weakening. At any rate the mob speedily dispursed and the axe and crow bar was heaved over the court yard fence after them.

That part of the revised scriptures will have to be revised for this part of the world, for there are personally known to be quite a number of 'old wine skins' hereabouts that are being constantly tested in this respect, and never an explosion has there been yet.

An old negro barber named Thomas Freeman, who had been keeping a barber shop on Ohio levee, several doers above Eighth street, for a number of years, was found dead in his chair by one of his customers yesterday afternoon. He lived very secluded, attending strictly to his business and, for all that was known, enjoyed life. The cause of his sudden death is a mystery.

A paper is being circulated in the city and is being numerously signed setting forth that Mr. Henry Stout, of this city, is a competent workman in masonry and thoroughly reliable in all his undertakings. The paper is to be used by Mr. Stout in furthering his chances to obtain the contract for rebuilding the Anna insane asylum. That Mr. Stout is, in every respect, able to satisty the best judges of work in his line, is an acknowledged fact wherever he is known.

The Cairo correspondent of the Chicago
Tribune in his account of the accident
which resulted fatally to young George
Merrian, says that it is thought death was
caused by the "chloroform that was given him." This is an error. Doctor Parker,
who dressed the boy's wounds, administered
no chloroform or anything else unto him.
The boy was, during the operation of amputating his fingers, in a stupor from which he did not awake. Nothing but a little liquor was given him, and that before he was brought into the doctor's office. It is the opinion of Doctor Parker that the boy died of cerebral hemorrhage.

It was rumored late last night that another attempt to do personal violence to the negro, Albert Hayes, would be made early this morning. That twelve men from Kentucky had been imported to do the job of hanging the young wretch. Up to this writing, half-past eleven o'clock, all is quiet and no attempt has been made to repeat the rather grotesque affair of the night before. That there is ample cause for indignation at the heinous crime of the youthful devil cannot be doubted, but it is also a crime to take him out of the hands of the law after he has been placed under lock and key with the intention of sending him prematurely into hades.

Albert Hayes, the young negro, whose blood was sought by a company of angry citizens night before last, was taken to the county court room for a preliminary examination yesterday afternoon. Esquire Osborn was present and held court. The negro was represented by Hon. D. T. Linegar and the people by City Attorney Hendricks. The prisoner waived an examination, and was held in bond in the sum of five hundred dollars for his appearance at the July term of the circuit court. He was very much scared at the attempt made upon his life the night before, and therefore he was not brought to the police court for trial.

—Paducah Enterprise: "Mr. and Mrs. Frank McKnight and little son, of Cairo, are in the city, guests of the Richmond House. Mr. McKnight is just home from Hot Springs, Ark., where he has been under treatment for rheumatism. Though much better, he is still compelled to use crutches, but hopes to be all right again in a very short time. His gallery in Cairo will be reopened about August 1st."

—Mr. John A. Reeve has gone into the furniture and auction buisness at the corner of Tenth street and Washington avenue. He says that he has permanently abandoned politics, but it is safe to predict that when he hears the fife and drum, and smells the powder of election canon and the odor of burning campaign lanterns, the old political Adam will rise again in him and induce him to run, if not for office, why, then, perhaps, only for fun.

A woman named Goulding was burned to death a day or two by the explosion of coal oil, which was sold for 130 fire test, but which proved to be only 105 when tested. The law of Kentucky does not permit the sale of any burning fluid for family use that will explode at less than one hundred and thirty degrees Fahrenheit. In Illinois this does not appear to be the case, as great quantities of coal oil of no more than one hundred and ten degrees fire test, are being daily sold in this city as well as elsewhere.

The Paducah Enterprise announces in large letters that the negro, who assaulted Mrs. Johnson in that city on Tuesday, was caught within six hours after the assault. That's nothing. Marshal Myers and Officers Olmsted and Tyler, of this city caught the negro who assaulted Mrs. Kobler in this city some time ago within four hours after the assault, and if it hadn't been for the bravery of Jailer Fitzerald and posse, the wretch would have been hung within six hours after he committed the crime.

Six prisoners broke jail at Tyler, Tex., making the third escape within a month.

For an assault on a soap peddler following his show, Adam Forepaugh was fined $24.65 by a justice at Black River Falls, Wis.

For an article attacking the army, a journalist of Pesth has been sentenced to four months' imprisonment and fined one thousand florins.

Jackson Eastman, a prominent business man of Norfolk, Va., died from a stab from a pocket knife in the hands of Thomas Donald.

Otto Tooker, a Boston youth of 13, shot and killed a companion, Gustave Buettner, a boy of 16, with a toy pistol. The boys had a quarrel.

A report from Piedras Negras states that several American engineers have been killed in Mexico in consequence of disputes regarding right of way.

H. L. Smith, who lives in jail at Tupelo, Miss., under sentence to be hanged on July 18, has eaten nothing for twelve days, and declares he will starve to death.

In an affray between whites and blacks at Columbia, Va., a negro named Bill Hackney was struck on the head with a pick-handle and flung out of a window fifteen feet from the ground.

ManSFIELD, who was stabbed some three weeks ago by a Chinese laundryman in a dispute over the price for washing a shirt, is dying at the county hospital, Chicago.

The police of Cincinnati have jailed the proprietor of a turf exchange and five of his clerks for selling pools. Another operator and two clerks were arrested for putting up a board for the sale of combination pools.

A notable feature of emigration statistics for 1880 is the great number of English people who have reached Castle Garden, Germany and Ireland head the list, as usual, and Sweeden follows, but the English immigrants number more than those from Austria, Hungary, Russia, France and Italy combined. No wonder the late Prime Minister of England felt called upon to belittle the United States in a wonderfully imaginative agricultural address.

The four Vanderbilt houses now building at New York are to be the finest of anything in the country, and it will be two years before any of them are ready to occupy. Although the architect has had six draughtsmen working for a year upon the plause of W. K. Vanderbilts' house, the details of the inside have not yet been considered. The sculptors and art workers are all brought from Europe, and interruptions constantly occur for want of some workman who cannot be found in the city. On W. H. Vanderbilts' house the tiling of the ground floor and the halls had to be made by the poet decorator, Morris in London.

Thomas, of Whitakers Thownship in Nash county, ware carried last before United States Commissioner at Raleigh, charged with obstructing the polls at the late elections they being judges. Chas. E. The Grange passed a general fence law to be voted on by counties, townships, or sections, wherever a majority of the qualified voters in either petitioned the county commissioners. They wished an agricultural board to be appointed by the Legislature, with a man each for cotton, tobacco, stock raising and grazing, horticulture, manufacturing and mining, and this board to elect the commissioner. They wished the land scrip from Congress to be applied exclusively to establishing an agricultural college in or near Raleigh. This subject was spoken to by Colonel Winston, Dr. Benbow, Mr. Williams and Worthy Master Cheek, of the Grange committee. They said it was the sentiment with but one dissenting voice, and that was Mr. Thigpen's. Mr. Thigpen said he was opposed to taking it from the University. Instead of Agricultural college in Raleigh, if necessary let the college be added to Chapel Hill. He wished it understood that he never was in college hall—had worked hard all his life. But he wanted his children at some other college than a mere agricultural school; he could teach them agriculture in the field. Col. Winston argued that the United States government might at any time demand of the State to refund this appropriation because of its being misapplied, as was the case in California under similar circumstances. It was taken from the university and put in an agricultural college to anticipate and guard against such a contingency. Char. Observer.

Notes from Indian Territory. CALDWELL, Ks., May 9.—Several cattle men arrived here from the Round Ups, in the Indian Territory, and report that the cattle are not badly scattered, and that they are in a better condition than could be expected. There is plenty of grass and water and the cattle are taking on fat very fast. Have had plenty of rain here. Wheat is beading out and corn is being cultivated, all reports to the contrary notwithstanding. The Indians in the Territory are quiet, showing no disposition to create trouble. MRS. STEIMAN.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LA CHOSSE, WI., May 9.—The examination of Mr. Stelman, charged with the murder of Mr. Siegbort, a prosperous merchant of Prairie du Chien, began at this place this morning. Mr. Stelman was rearrooted this morning at Prairie du Chien and taken to a Justice Court to be examined, and the Court removed to the Court-House to enable the crowd to gain admittance to hear the proceedings. The excitement is intense both in this city and in Prairie du Chien. The case attracts much attention on account of Mr. Stelman being one of our largest business-men. In the evidence taken to-day some important facts were made known, but no case of blackmail has yet been proven. Mrs. Stelman has an able counsel, who believes he will be fully vindicated on the charge, which is made by one Smith, claiming to be one of Pinkerton's detectives. Various rumors are alloyed as to the cause of the supposed murder, and further developments in the case are awaited with anxiety. The examination will probably require two days, as the defense have not yet done anything in the way of testimony.

STAR ROUTE.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa., May 9.—Joseph R. Black, William R. Cason, and Joseph Blackman, charged with defrauding the Government in mail contracts, were arraigned for final hearing before United States Commissioner Smith this afternoon. Their counsel stated that he had been informed that Henry C. Arbuckle would also be present, but that defendant failed to appear. The Commissioner stated it was evident from the testimony that Black was the principal in the transaction, but the others were equally responsible. The prisoners theroupon were held in $5,000 ball each for their appearance at the coming term of the United States District Court, which begins on Monday next. This afternoon Henry Arbuckle, charged with being one of the star-route conspirators, surrendered to the United States Marshal, waived a hearing, and was held in $5,000 ball.

BURGLARS AND SAFE-BLOWERS.
LITTLE ROCK, Ark., May 9.—An organized band of burglar and safe-blowers has been operating through Arkansas the past six months. Safes at Princeton, Danville, and Toledo were robbed recently. Chief-of-Police Counts to-night arrested E. Dryson, Charles Thomas, and James L. Reeny at the house of a colored woman, charged with being members of the gang. The same parties were arrested some time since for robbing a safe at Princeton, but managed to escape. The prisoners are desperate looking men, reluctant, and refuse to tell anything. The officers are confident they have the right parties.

A THRILLING FIGHT.

A Savage Maddog Attacks a Girl—A Man Goes to Her Rescue and Is Severely Bitten in the Desperate Struggle That Follows—Other Persons Bitten by the Infurited Beast.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Baltimore, Md., May 9.—The northern section of this city was thrown into the wildest state of excitement by the terrible attack on a number of persons by an infuriated bulldog suffering with hydrophobia. For some time past Mr. James M. Epply, who resides on the northern boundary of the city, has been the owner of two of those dangerous beasts, and has kept them confined in the roar yard attached to his residence. This afternoon one of the dogs forcously attacked the other, and, while they were engaged in a desperate fight, a colored girl belonging to the house wont to the back door to endeavor to separate them, but no sooner did she make her appearance than one of them, frothing at the mouth, seized her by the left log and toro a great piece of flesh from the calf of the limb. Stricken with terror and pain, the girl screamed for help, and Mr. William Thompson, who was passing at the time, came to her assistance and fired at the animal through the fence with his revolver. The ball missed its mark, and Mr. Thompson then climbed to the top of the fence to secure a better aim for his next shot. No sooner did the maddoned beast see him than it looped for his throat, and getting a savage hold, together they fell off the fence into the street. Mr. Thompson, who is a powerful man, fought desperately, and finally succeeded in getting away from the animal, but not until his coat and short were torn from him and he was severally bitten in the throat and breast. The dog then ran madly down Maryland avenue, and his next victim was a child named Eddie Simm, son of one of our leading dry-goods microhants. Dashing at the boy, the dog throw him down and bit and toro the flesh from a dozen parts of his body. Painting and bleeding, the child was picked up and carried to his father's residence close by. A crowd had by this time gathered in pursuit of the dog, but was not finally disposed of, although a dozen shots were fired at him, several of which wounded him, until he had severally bitten a colored boy named Richard Franklin, a distance of five or six squares from where the infurred boast had started on his blood-thirsty flight.

CINCINNATI'S MAYOR.

Ha Has Become Very Unpopular with the Democrats—They Propose to Hold a Public Meeting and Denounce His Conduct Since His Elevation to Office.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

CINCINNATI, O., May 23.—A hall has been hired and a meeting called by a number of Democrats of this city for the purpose of denouncing the policy of the Reform Mayor, Mr. William Means. The meeting will be held on Saturday night next, and is called by some of the most prominent Democrats who are accustomed to mix in local politics. The complaint against Mayor Means is, that he is untrue to the party who elected him, and it is proposed to formally announce his disloyalty at a public meeting called for that purpose, and to give him back to the easy-going and wealthy clique from whom he came. The Mayor was elected six weeks ago by a combination of the Democratic party and a considerable class of Republicans who were anxious to see certain reforms carried out touching liquor-selling and the observance of the Sabbath. Means, it was thought by the Democrats, could be easily handled, and half a dozen of the old party leaders each flattered himself that he would be the new Mayor's confidential adviser and the power behind the throne. When elected, however, Mr. Means announced that he wanted no advice from anybody, and, though supported by the whole Democratic party, would give none of its leaders a hearing as to how the patronage should be distributed. A few Democratic politemen received appointments, but it was entirely through their own efforts. Those who depended upon the leaders of the party for recommendation and assistance had no attention paid to their applications. "The same was true of applicants for other offices, and the rank and file of the party, as well as its leaders, have naturally became very sore, and the step which they have now resolved to take has been talked of for some time. The Reform Republicans have been better satisfied with the Mayor's course, for the reason that there has been some effort at reform, although the results are hardly appreciable. The Mayor is a life-long Democrat, but knows nothing about politics, and, being of an obstinate disposition, he got his party by the ears at the very outset. The effect, of course, has been to greatly strengthen the Republicans. The Democratic victory at the spring election, unexpectedly to everybody, is proving to be one of the best things for the Republican party that could have happened.

Some time ago there arrived in this city a young man who gave his name as Walch de Serrant. He said he was a count, all the way from France, and as his manners were very smooth and ingratiating, his story obtained wide credence. He fell into bad ways, however, and in consequence became intimately acquainted with the criminal laws of Texas, Arkansas and Louisiana. The editor of the Little Rock Gazette "wrote up" the court in a very laughable manner, and the victim swore that he would be avenged upon the writer as soon as he had righted himself in the eyes of the public. Circumstances intervened, however, preventing the execution of this laudable resolve. A very short time after his arrival in the Crescent City, he indulged in one of his peculiar pranks, called in legal phraseology grand larceny, and was taken before a court, tried, found guilty, and sentenced to five years in the State penitentiary.

His counsel took an appeal to the Supreme Court, and yesterday the verdict and judgment of the lower court was affirmed. Justice Todd, who read the decision of the Supreme Court, took occasion to say in the course of his remarks:

We have closely scrutinized the proceedings pertaining to this prosecution, and we cannot find a single right or privilege guaranteed to an accused by law that was denied the defendant, but on the contrary that every means of defense in the power of the court was afforded him, and we find no error or irregularity in any part of the proceeding.

The count will take a visit up the river as far as Baton Rouge, where in the privacy and reclusion of the penitentiary or work on the road he will have ample time and opportunity to perfect his bellicose arrangements for the annihilation of the Arkansas editor who gave him such a beautiful send off in his paper.

The Sparta Rural Times gives the following account of the killing of the colored boy who raped and murdered a lithe colored girl some weeks ago: "Before our last Saturday's paper containing an account of the horrible double crime committed in our parish last Sunday week, had time to reach its readers, the perpetrator, Cherry Nichols, was dangling between earth and heaven with several bullet holes in his body. Saturday night last, at about 11 o'clock, Mr. Whitlow, the sheriff, was aroused by a party of six men who informed him that they were new comers in the lower part of this parish and that they had a hog thief, who they called Dock, in their possession, and wished to put him in jail. Not suspicioning anything at all, the sheriff went at once and unlocked the jail and ordered Dock, who by this time was all in tears at the idea of going in prison, to walk in. But Dock wouldn't walk worth a cent. By this time a perfect little army of both white and colored men, who had concealed themselves in a clump of woods near the jail, had completely surrounded the jail doors when Mr. Whitlow, was told that Dock was one of their citizens—they wanted Cherry Nichols, and Cherry Nichols they would have. They were remonstrated with for several minutes, half an hour perhaps, but without effect. For one man to undertake to control forty or fifty armed and determined men, and that too, after the prison doors were thrown open, would have been worse than folly, so the sheriff surrendered the boy into their hands. He was made secure and marched off in the direction of Mount Lebanon. He was found about six miles north of here in an old field last Monday hanging to a tree literally shot to pieces. The same day Dr. Harrell, the coroner, summoned a jury and repaired to the scene, where a post mortem examination was held over the dead

—At Major J. B. Rawls' headquarters in Fort Brooke we saw an antiquated curiosity the other afternoon in the shape of a small swivel cannon which had been picked up recently on a reef near Tortugas in ten feet water. This gun is about three feet long, with a bore of about an inch and a half. It was pretty well incrusted with a coral growth of from one to three inches in thickness, showing that it had been a long, long time since it found a resting place in the Gulf. It may be a relic of the buccaneers or of some of the hardy adventurers of the long ago who sought the new world for conquest or plunder. The Major had also a preserved porcupine fish whose skin was studded with sharp spines of from one to two inches long. This curious fish is short, thick and broad, and this specimen when caught must have weighed 6 or 8 pounds. — Tampa Tribune.

dickerson-leesburg.A2:
A Florida Lynching.
JACKSONVILLE, FLA., July 16.—Some weeks ago J. J. Dickinson, Jr., son of General Dickinson, late Adjutant-General of Florida, had a difficulty with a saloon-keeper named Beach in Leesburg, Sumter county. It was apparently adjusted at the time, but was renewed by Dickinson last Tuesday, when he took advantage of Beach and fired two shots from a double-barrelled gun at him and made his escape, supposing he had killed him. Beach was severely but not dangerously wounded. Dickinson was captured and lodged in Leesburg jail. At 2 o'clock yesterday morning an armed and disguised mob of twenty-five men appeared at the jail, overpowered the jailer, and shot Dickinson twice in prison. They then took him outside and riddled him with bullets.

The Lynching of Young Dickison.
In our telegraphic columns appears a dispatch from Jacksonville, Fla., announcing the death of J. J. Dickison, Jr., son of Gen. Dickison, late Adjutant General of Florida, at the hands of a mob, who took him from the jail at Leesburg, where he had been confined on the charge of having shot a saloon-keeper named Beach. This young man will doubtless be remembered by many of our citizens. His father, General Dickison, shortly after the war, removed from Florida to Savannah, and for a number of years carried on the factorage and commission business on the Bay. Young Dickison was a clerk with his father, and his career here made him generally known. Gen. Dickison returned to Florida, and was appointed Adjutant General under Governor Drew, and is a gentleman not only highly thought of here, but in Florida.
dickerson-leesburg.A12:
John Dickison Killed.
We learn from a detailed account of the affair in the Union of Sunday, that J. J. Dickison, Jr., the son of General J. J. Dickison, of Quincy, who had become engaged in a personal difficulty with a man named Beach at Leasburg, at whom he had fired, was taken from the jail, under the erroneous impression that Beach was fatally wounded, and lynched, by a party of armed and disguised men.

This unfortunate and horrible affair is the first instance known in the State where there was so little shadow of excuse for arbitrary or violent measures; and brings upon the aged surviving parents of the victim a sorrow that will follow them through life, and in which they have the sincerest sympathy and confluence of a large circle of devoted friends in this section where they have resided so long.

Words fail to adequately express the horror and condemnation felt by all good citizens for the commission of such a crime against law, good order and civilization.

For the past three weeks our town has been under excitement over the first attempt of Mr. J. J. Dickison, Jr., to kill Mr. Lewis Beach.

We will here give a short sketch of his career in Leesburg previous to this time. More than a year ago he came to Leesburg, having to secretly leave Quincy for shooting a negro. As he became acquainted with the people, it was found he had a generous disposition, but with it he was tyrannical and overbearing, especially when drinking. He had not been here long before it was evident to everyone's mind that he was a desperate man, and was pronounced by the community to be a desperado and outlaw, as he had defied the law on every occasion. His career was such that people feared him; they were uneasy whenever he came to town, for as soon as he began to drink he began to fuss with any and everybody, and no one knew at what time he would attempt to kill them. About the middle of June he attempted to draw the town Marshal into a difficulty. He drew his pistol and asked him to do the same, cursing him, calling him a coward and defying him to attempt to arrest him. The Marshal told him not to shoot; that he had nothing against him, and did not want to arrest him. We were present on this occasion, and Colonel Smith also. We both did all in our power to get him off, but did not succeed until he had insulted the Marshal in every way possible.

The particulars in the affair with Mr. Beach are as follows: On the 28th of June Mr. Dickison came to the barroom of Mr. S. W. Wallace, where Mr. Beach was staying, and threw an empty beer keg through the door and blinds, making a fearful racket. Mr. Beach came out and accused him of the act. Dickison denied it, and at the same time drew his pistol and asked Beach if he wished to shoot it out. Beach saw the weapon in his face and drew his also. Dickison seeing that Beach had an equal showing with him, proposed to replace the pistols and let the matter drop. Beach was only too glad to comply, and, believing Dickison to be a man of honor, and relying on what he said, accepted the treaty of peace; but Dickison only sought to gain the advantage, for no sooner did Beach put up his pistol than Dickison drew his and fired, fortunately without effect. Beach returned the fire, striking Dickison in the arm. Dickison stepped aside, out of range of Beach's pistol, and fired, but again without effect. Dickison then ran, and Beach followed him, firing two other shots, but missed, when Dickison disappeared in the dark. Dickison was arrested the day after, and set at liberty under simply a peace bond of $500. His wound was cared for by Dr. Stevens, and when he left town he said that the affair was not through with, although he had sent for Beach, made friends and expressed much sorrow at what had occurred. This statement is certified to by several witnesses. Dickison came to town several times after and acted in a way to lead every one to believe that he intended to attempt Beach's life. The suspicions of the people were so thoroughly aroused that they went to Beach and warned him not to have any intercourse with Dickison. Beach listened to this counsel only partially, for on Monday night, July 11th, Dickison called Beach out back of Baer's store to converse with him. The discourse was strictly of a friendly nature, which threw Beach entirely off his guard. Dickison stepped off from Beach about thirty feet and began to feel around as if looking for something. Beach asked him what he was doing, when he said: "Beach, God d—n you, you have said enough to me," and raised a shot gun, which he had concealed, and fired. Beach received the load in the shoulder, and Dickison, thinking he had killed him, ran off. Beach gave the alarm, and the Mayor sent a posse of men in hot pursuit, for it was the most cold blooded attempt to murder ever perpetrated in this county. Beach's shoulder was filled with buckshot, and two of his arm bones were broken. He is now under the treatment of Dr. Stevens, and is doing as well as could be expected.

Dickison had made threats to take the lives of no less than six of our good citizens, for no reason whatever. The names of these parties we could mention if necessary. One of the parties in particular he said he intended to kill while asleep in bed. The day he shot Beach, while coming to town he shot at a negro just to try the gun
One of the parties in particular he said he intended to kill while asleep in bed. The day he shot Beach, while coming to town he shot at a negro just to try the gun he shot Beach with. He hailed the negro and told him he wished to try his gun. The negro jumped behind a tree, which saved his life. The load from his gun was buried in the tree behind which the negro stood.

With the attempt to murder Beach and knowing the threats he had made, the citizens determined to capture him if possible. The Sheriff summoned a posse and began the pursuit Tuesday morning. The woods around his house were scoured and he was routed Tuesday noon, but the party did not get up with him. They learned that he had crossed the Ocklawah river, secured a mule and was heading for Ocala, and the chase was hotly pursued on horseback, about twelve in the party. They finally struck his trail, and after riding hard all Wednesday night found him at daylight Thursday morning. Dickison was asleep in a house, which was surrounded, when he was summoned to surrender. He had a shot-gun with him, and for a short while he thought of making a rush on the party, kill as many as he could and make his escape. Knowing this would be certain death to himself, he finally surrendered. He was brought to Leesburg Thursday evening and lodged in jail with a strong guard placed over him, and now we are palmed to chronicle his doom. About two o'clock Friday morning a masked body of men, numbering between twenty-five and thirty, overpowered the guards, forced them to open the door, and shot Dickison with double-barrel guns.

We do not approve of lynch law, and are sorry that this community had to resort to such extreme measures. We have sketched the foregoing short account of Dickison's career in Leesburg to let the world know why such severe measures were resorted to, and as the deed is done a number of our most influential citizens have requested us to give an impartial statement of Mr. Dickison's career, showing that this county is not lawless, but law-abiding, and that they feel much relieved at the death of Mr. Dickison, for no man's life with whom he came in contact was safe.

do, condemn and abhor the crime of assassination, but what has led to the crime? Innocence, sweetness, kindness, generosity? No, none of these, but oppression so bitter, so galling to the soul, so rending to the heart, that for years men and women—persons of station and refinement—have taken their destinies in their hands, ready to give up life so that they might avenge upheaped injustice, and deliver their weeping, suffering people from the arrogant brutality that has pursued them with deliberate, cold, black, passionless malice. Is it nothing to awake in the morning and find that your dearest have been stolen from you in the night by the hand of power, aud thrust without trial, without even pretense of justice, into a jail to herd, it may be for years, with convicts, the outcasts of the earth, in a prison. Do you know how such crimes, perpetrated by the hand of power, sears every fiber, rives every tender spot in the human organization, turning the milk to gall and freezing every fond and delicate chord of feeling to iron, to the hardness of hate? A silly rumor was, a few days ago, given publication by a Republican paper to the effect that Senator Harris, of this State, could be counted upon to vote with Davis and Mahone in securing to that party the reorganization of the senate. This, in view of the consistent record of the senator, was so manifestly absurd that no one of his friends thought of denying it, or, indeed, of noticing it in any way, but Ben Hill, of Georgia, in the course of his onslaught on Mahone, on Monday, alluded to it, whereupon Senator Harris expressed his regret that Mr. Hill had thought proper to dignify the miserable newspaper twaddle in regard to his (Mr. Harris's) political position. There was not a Democrat or Republican in the country who knew him who ever doubted what his political positions were. The matter was unworthy of notice." So we thought at the time, for if Senator Harris has one virtue more prominent than another it is that of consistency as an unswerving Democrat.

GENERAL UPTON, who committed suicide yesterday at San Francisco, was one of the best tacticians in the army and very soon after the civil war published a work on tactics which is still in use with the militia, as well as the army of the United States. He also wrote a critical and very valuable work on the condition, formation and discipline of the several European armies, and besides enjoyed an enviable reputation as an officer and gentleman. Grief for his deceased wife it is supposed induced the rash act that has robbed his country of a gallant soldier. General Upton entered the army from West Point, and was commissioned as second lieutenant of the Fourth artillery on the sixth of May, 1861, and subsequently served in the infantry as well as artillery. During the war he distinguished himself as a brave and skillful officer and was rewarded by rapid promotions, being mustered out of the volunteer service on the thirtieth of April, 1866, with the brevet rank of major-general.

THE result of the meeting of the Mississippi Greenbackers and Republicans held recently at the Peabody hotel has at last cropped out in the statement that a delegation of Mississippi Republicans have laid before the President a plan for carrying the State by uniting with the Greenbackers, being convinced of the uselessness of trying the strength of a straight Republican ticket again. Their plan is to run Ex-Governor Alcorn for governor next fall and give the Greenbackers the rest of the State ticket, provided the President will give them the Federal patronage to promote their plans. Thus warned the Democrats should unite, and prepare for a very sharp and close contest.

A RAVISHER

Meets His Deservings at the Hands of an Infuriated Mob.

HANDSBORO, MISS., March 15.—Ed Turner, a negro confined in the jail at Mississippi City for ravishing the person of Mrs. Mike McIntosh, a white lady living on Wolf river, near Pass Christian, Harrison county, on the 5th, was taken out of jail last Saturday night at 11 o'clock by a party of fifty or sixty armed men and hung to an oak tree near Le Garden hotel. Rather than have the doors broken down with axes the jailer gave up the keys. Coroner J. T. Baldwin impaneled the jury early this morning, but the body was not taken down until 3 o'clock this evening, owing to some misunderstanding of the law in the premises. The action of the lynchers meets the approval of all good citizens.

fritz-w-haas-union-1881-03.A1:
LATE NEWS ITEMS.
GEN. COLLEY, with six companies of British soldiers, suffered a most disastrous defeat at the hands of the Boers at Spitzkop, on the 27th ult., Gen. Colley himself being killed, together with the greater portion of his command, which consisted of twenty-two officers and 627 men. The British occupied the summit of a hill, up which the Boers charged four times, the last attempt to capture it being successful, as is alleged, solely on account of the British running out of ammunition.

PRINCESS AUGUSTA VICTORIA, the bride-elect of the eldest son of the Crown Prince of Germany, arrived at Berlin on the 26th, and was publicly received by the Emperor and royal family. The occasion was made a grand fete day, business throughout the city being suspended and the streets and buildings decorated in holiday attire. The religious ceremony of the marriage was performed on the evening of the 27th, a grand court reception being afterward held, followed by a State banquet.

FRITZ W. HAAS and Catherine Hoffart, his alleged paramour, confined in the Franklin County Jail at Union, Mo., under indictment for the murder of Mrs. Haas, narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of an infuriated crowd. Under cover of darkness the officers finally succeeded in getting the prisoners out of town and conveying them to St. Louis, where they are now safe at least from mob violence.

THE Catholic Orphan Asylum at Hyde Park, Scranton, Pa., partially burned on the night of the 27th, causing the death of seventeen of the inmates, all children. The victims were locked in their rooms on the third floor, and the dense smoke and flames rendered it impossible for the sisters to effect their release. Only two were touched by the flames, the others being suffocated.

A MEXICAN named Marino, another of the alleged murderers of Col. Potter, was forcibly taken from the Jail at Albuquerque, N. Mex., and hanged by the vigilantes.

THE Court-House at Greenwood, Sebastian County, Ark. and all its contents
The Court-House at Greenwood, Sebastian County, Ark., and all its contents were totally destroyed by fire on the night of the 24th. Incendiarism is suspected.

The Senate, on the 26th, after a protracted session, passed the River and Harbor bill, the vote being 32 yeas to 12 nays. Those voting nay were Messrs. Bailey, Bayard, Blair, Dawes, Eaton, Harris, Jones (Nev.), Kernan, Logan, Pendleton, Saulsbury and Wallace. The House completed the Sundry Civil Appropriation bill in Committee of the Whole, and then took a recess till Monday without taking a vote. The bill for the relief of settlers upon absentee Shawnee lands in Kansas passed both Houses. The conference committee on the Apportionment bill did not come to an agreement.

PERSONAL AND GENERAL.

MRS. DEBORAH MERRILL, aged 54, living with her son Charles, aged 23, at Week's Mills, in Kennebec County, Me., was recently murdered by the latter and her body chopped in pieces, partially burned, and then buried in a manure heap, where it was found some days later. The inhuman son has been arrested, and is now confined in Augusta Jail, where he was taken to avoid lynching. He confesses having killed his mother by striking her on the head with a hammer and then disposing of her body in the manner stated. The murderer has long borne an unenviable reputation among his neighbors, and had frequently quarreled with his mother, who was herself something of a virago. There is an elder Merrill, who was absent from home, engaged in cutting wood at Moosehead Lake.

The usual Mardi Gras celebrations took place in New Orleans, Memphis and Shreveport. The weather was fine and the attendance unusually large, especially of Northern visitors at New Orleans.

It is reported that the Crow Indians have declared a war of extermination against the Flatheads and all tribes north of the Mussellshell, owing to raids on their territory by predatory bands from these tribes. They have appealed to the Government for assistance, but Gen. Terry has given instructions that the military of that district shall take no further action in the controversy than to bring about an adjustment of the trouble, which threatens to be very serious.

A NUMBER of prominent Chicago physicians, interviewed for the Tribune, gave it as their opinion that the disease known as winter cholera, which has been prevailing to an alarming extent in that city during the winter, is traceable to the extensive use of butterine. Dealers in the unsavory article are being prosecuted for selling it without being properly labeled. It is said the cheap restaurants and boarding-houses are the principal consumers of butterine.

WILL LOWREY, a young man, son of a wealthy widow residing near Bloomington, Ill., was engaged in cleaning his revolver the other day, when his sister, abeautiful young lady of 20, passing near him, he playfully pointed at her the supposed unloaded pistol and pulled the trigger. To his unspeakable horror the pistol was discharged, and his sister fell to the floor. Examination showed that the bullet had entered beside the spinal column about eight inches below the shoulder, ranging upward. Surgeons were at once sent for and they pronounced the wound fatal. The young man, on learning the terrible result of his foolishness, declared he would kill himself, and was only prevented from doing so by the interference of those near him.

THE trial of the Sprague divorce suit has begun at Providence, R. I.

GOVERNOR FOSTER commuted to imprisonment for life the sentence of John Welsh, who was to have been hanged at Fremont, O., on the 4th.

A COLORED woman living near Todd's Point, Shelby County, Ky., locked her three children in the cabin and went away. During her absence the cabin burned with its imprisoned inmates.

A Swiss colony has purchased 10,000 acres of land near London, Laurel County, Ky. Forty families are expected immediately and they will be followed by more when suitable locations are procured.

THE Chicago boiler-makers, shipcarpenters and caulkers are still holding out for advanced wages.

ANOTHER terrible snowstorm prevailed throughout the Northwest on the night of the 2d, completely blocking railway traffic. MRS. ELIZABETH PERCEVIEL, proprietress of the English Kitchen restaurant, New Orleans, was shot and mortally wounded by her divorced husband, Richard Stevens, as the Mardi Gras procession was passing her place of business.

granville-harrel-1880-12-18.A1:
HORRIBLE HOMICIDE!
An Old Citizen Murdered With An Ax.
On Thursday morning, about 11 o'clock, the startling intelligence rapidly passed from lip to lip that Mr. David Simmons, who kept a meat market in West Jackson, had just been killed by a negro man in his employ named Granville Harrell. As soon as it was known that the report was well founded, and being interested in obtaining the facts, we proceeded to the place of this sad occurrence, and, after interviewing two or three reliable parties, gleaned the following particulars:

The man Granville had been for a long time in the employ of Mr. Simmons, and there existed some trouble in regard to their financial affairs. This seems to have brought to the surface the old Satan in the negro. On the morning of the homicide they were doing some work about the premises, and occasionally quarreling over their differences; while they were thus engaged, and at a moment when Mr. S. was not expecting an
the forehead, crushing the skull in both instances, which caused his death in a very short time. The negro ran off carrying the ax with him, which he still had when captured by officer Fitzpatrick and others. By this time excitement was running high, and a mob was gathering, but the officer, recognizing the spirit of the law as to the protection of its prisoner in such cases, hurried the culprit to jail, and thus barely succeeded in snatching him from the hands of the enraged populace who probably would have instantly meted out summary justice without judge or jury.

The following is the verdict of the jury of inquest:

We the jury, empanneled to sit on inquest over the body of David Simmons, Sr., find, after a full and careful examination, by the testimony submitted to us, that he came to his death by means of blows from an ax in the hands of Granville Harrell, and we believe that the said Granville Harrell is guilty of premeditated murder. J. W. LESTER, Foreman, H. D. LESTER, T. J. HARDY, A. G. GAYLE, G. M. DENHAM, E. N. COLLINS. J. D. MONAHAN, J. P., and acting Coroner.

The remains of Mr. Simmons were consigned to their last resting place yesterday evening at 4 o'clock, followed by the Fire Department and a large concourse of citizens of Jackson.
granville-harrel-1880-12-18.A2:
A CRUEL AND FOUL MURDER.
One of Our Oldest and Best Citizens Slain in Cold Blood Without Cause.
The Assassination of Mr. David Simmons by a Negro Named Granville Harrell.
The community was shocked Thursday morning by a report that Mr. David Simmons, residing near Jackson, had been foully and brutally murdered by a negro man in his employment named Granville Harrell. There had been scarcely an unpleasant word spoken by Mr. Simmons to the negro, and he was totally unconscious that he harbored a revengeful feeling towards him. While his back was turned towards the negro, the latter struck him a deadly blow on the head with an ax, and repeated it while he was down. The skull was crushed at each blow. After committing the deed, the negro went to the house and told the daughter of Mr. Simmons (the mother being absent) what he had done, and when reproached by the grief stricken daughter with tears and lamentation for killing her father, the fiend became furious and lifted his ax to strike her, but fortunately it was seized by his wife just in time to save her life. When arrested the murderer confessed, and boasted of what he had done, in language the most horrible and profane.

The following was the verdict of the jury of inquest:

We the jury, empanneled to sit on inquest over the body of David Simmons, Sr., find, after a full and careful examination, by the testimony submitted to us, that he came to his death by means of blows from an ax in the hands of Granville Harrell, and we believe that the said Granville Harrell is guilty of premeditated murder.

J. W. LESTER, Foreman,
H. D. LESTER,
T. J. HARDY,
A. G. GAYLE,
G. M. DENHAM,
E. N. COLLINS,
J. D. MONAHAN, J. P.
And Acting Coroner.
THE MURDERER.

Apprehending that the indignation of the community would overleap restraint, and lynch the assassin, Sheriff Morrison took the precaution to remove him early Thursday night from the jail here to the one at Raymond. We learn that on Saturday night a numerous body of persons, whose names to this writer are unknown, went to the Raymond jail, overpowered the jailer, seized the murderer and hung him. He repeated his confession, and at the same time made some statements implicating other parties which for prudential considerations we will not print.

MR. DAVID SIMMONS
the victim of this atrocious crime, was born in Germany on the 24th of April 1824. In his youth he immigrated to Jackson, where he has lived ever since. In 1846 he married Miss Denham, who, together with a family of sons and daughters, have survived him. There never lived a more upright, honorable man than David Simmons. He was kind to his family and just to everybody. He never gave offence, and would suffer wrong rather than engage in a quarrel. He was public-spirited, and loved to do charitable deeds. Fifteen orphan children were cared for and raised by him and his estimable wife. Without a moment's warning, he was deprived of his life on earth, but there is reason to hope that he has entered upon life of immortal bliss beyond the grave.

Mr. Simmons was buried with the honors which such a life as he had lived deserved. The Fire Department and an immense course of citizens followed his remains to the grave.
granville-harrel-1880-12-18.A3:
A Murderer Lynched.
The Northern Republican papers are now furnished material for another Southern outrage. Last Thursday, in Jackson, a negro named Granville Harrell, for some imaginary offense, killed his employer, David Simmons, with an axe, splitting his head open at one blow. He was arrested and put in jail, but the Sheriff fearing he would be lynched moved him to the Raymond jail. The friends of the murdered man, on Saturday night last, took the murderer out of his cell, and hung him near the town. Sunday morning he was buried by direction of the coroner, whose jury returned a verdict exhonerating the officers from any blame and stating that the perpetrators were unknown. The mob was composed of whites and blacks, numbering one hundred and fifty.
granville-harrel-1880-12-18.A7:
Swift Retribution.
Granville Harrell who murdered Mr. David Simmons last week with an ax, was unceremoniously taken from the jail at Raymond, last Saturday night, and hung by a body of about one hundred men. The Gazette brought to us yesterday a detail of particulars, and confession of the prisoner, in which he fully acknowledged his unmitigated guilt as the perpetrator of this horrible deed; but as our space is limited, and the whole account contains nothing more than what was embraced in our report last week, and Granville's confession here on the day of arrest, we deem it useless to publish more than the verdict of the Jury of inquest, which is as follows:

We the jury summoned on the inquest of Granville Harrell, a prisoner confined in the county jail, after hearing the testimony of the witnesses, found that he was taken from the county jail by a mob, estimated at from 75 to 100 unknown men, and found outside the corporate limits of the town of Raymond, near Snake Creek, hanging by the neck; and,

We further exonerate the Sheriff and his deputies, who were overpowered by the mob, and compelled to give up up the keys of the jail.

granville-harrel-1880-12-18.A8:
A Fatal Locality.
The Raymond Gazette, in speaking of the spot where Granville Harrell was hung by a mob for the killing of Mr. Simmons, gives this bit of history:

In the year 1747, on the same road, not more than fifty yards below the tree on which Harrell was hung, Mr. J. W. Stewart, then Circuit Clerk of the county, was thrown from his horse and instantly killed. Fifty feet east of this spot in 1862 a negro was taken from from the jail and lynched in the same manner as Harrell. Two hundred yards south, nearer the town, in the field of Dr. Latimer, a mob shot and killed a negro, in 1866. Fifty feet west of this spot in 1875, a negro implicated in the famous Clinton riot, was taken from from the court house by unknown but infuriated parties and shot to death. Thus, in the same locality, no less than five different men have perished.
granville-harrel-1880-12-18.A9:
Negro Hung.
A Jackson telegram of the 19th to the New Orleans Picayune says: On Thursday evening, the 16th instant, one Granville Harrell, colored, murdered David Simmons, an old and respected citizen of this place. The fowl murder, it seems was unprovoked. Harrell was at once locked up in the county jail at this place. The sheriff, fearing mob violence, quietly took the prisoner to Raymond, eighteen miles west of here, where he was again confined, until last night, when a mob of fifty masked men overpowered the jailor, brought Harrell out and hung him to a tree a short distance from the jail. Harrell confessed his crime prior to the arrest, and boastingly said he cared nothing for the consequences.

A Murderer Lynched.
Granville Harrel, a negro, was lynched at Raymond, Miss., for the murder of an old and respectable white man named David Simmons, with an ax. After Harrel had committed the deed he went to Simmons' home and told his (Simmons') daughter that her father was lying out in the road, and if she wanted his body, she had better go and get it, adding that he had committed the deed. Harrel made a terrible resistance when the mob attempted to take him. Clasping his arms about a post, it took the combined efforts of fifteen men to detach his hold.

CIVIL SERVICE REFORM.
A Civil Service Reform Association has been organized in New York, the object of which is to establish a system of appointment, promotion and removal in the Civil Service, founded upon the principle that public office is a public trust, admission to which should depend upon proved fitness. To this end it is said the Association will demand that appointments to subordinate executive offices, with such exceptions, as may be expedient, not inconsistent with the principle already mentioned, shall be made from persons whose fitness has been ascertained by competitive examinations open to all applicants properly qualified, and that removals shall be made for legitimate cause only; such as dishonesty, negligence or inefficiency, but not for political opinion or refusal to render party service; and advocate all other appropriate measures for securing integrity, intelligence, efficiency, good order and due discipline in the Civil Service. Annual dues two dollars. Those who want to "jine" can pitch in. We don't.

Mr. J. B. Simmons was brutally murdered near Raymond, a few days ago, by a colored man named Granville Harrell. The murderer was arrested, confessed the crime, and was put in jail. That night, a party of unknown men took him from the jail by force and hung him to a limb, where he was found next morning very dead.

An attempt was made to wreck the express train for robbery, near Milwaukee, early Sunday morning. The first to reach the scene was a freight train, which was thrown off the track by obstructions. The thieves, however, compelled the unfortunate train hands to fork over.

Miss Mildred Lee, daughter of Gen. Robert E. Lee, is in Staunton, Va., the guest of Mrs. John B. Baldwin. Miss Lee has traveled nearly all over the world, and never heard the "Pinafore" until she heard it in Staunton the other night.

The Republican Union, of Missouri, a colored organization, has issued a call for a Colored National Convention, to assemble in Washington City, March 3, 1881, to demand a recognition of their race in the civil regulations of the government.

THE CITY-HALL.
THERE were thirty-eight deaths reported at the Health Office yesterday.

GEN. LIEB says that he will bring his slander-charge against Mr. Cragin before the new grand jury.

"The Factory Inspectors last week examined seventy-two factories, 393 stores, and made forty-four examinations of a miscellaneous character. In the places inspected there are 2,159 persons. There were twenty special examinations made. There were served thirty-six notices, and thirty-seven nuisances were abated.

A clerk in the employ of a Stock-Yards firm writes to Mayor Harrison suggesting that passengers who ride on the street-cars on the 25d inst. pay a fare of 10 cents each, the extra five cents to form a fund towards giving the drivers and conductors each a Christmas present. The suggestion is a good one, but the question is, How could it be carried out?

MAYOR HARRISON was still non-committal yesterday as to what his action would be on the Mutual Union pole ordinance. The Mayor was still in consultation with Prof. Barrett, President Evans, and Mr. Field, and there are those who say that the Mayor has stated that he is afraid that he will have to allow the ordinance to become a law, from all the evidence that he had before him.

THERE were five deaths from and eight new cases of small-pox reported yesterday. The new cases were reported from the northeast corner of Thirty-fifth street and Indiana avenue, No. 696 Noble, No. 2311 Hanover, No. 90 Lurrabee, No. 66 North Market, No. 421 Lurrabee streets, No. 690 Milwaukee and No. 165蒲堡 avenues. The deaths occurred at No. 194 North avenue, No. 901 West Eighteenth street, and No. 1075 Oakley avenue, at the Hospital, child taken from corner of Bissell and Clay street, and No. 386 Clarke street.

The Committee on Streets and Alleys South, met and recommended the repeal of the ordinance of 1875 for the opening of a street between Langley and Cottage Grove avenues, from Egan avenue to Thirty-ninth street. The committee recommended the improvement of Wabush avenue, from Twenty-second to Thirty-fifth street, with asphaltum blocks and stone sidewalks of a uniform width, and a like improvement for Thirty-fifth street, from State to

Michigan avenue, thus making a double connection with Thirty-fifth street boulevard. The matter of changing the name of State street to Broadway was laid over for one week. The Indiana State Line Railroad ordinance was also laid over for one week.

All who come to the Health Office have to run afoul of small-pox victims. These unfortunates, who linger about cheap lodgings and restaurants, having nowhere else to go, are trotted to the City-Hall, where they are compelled to remain, Dr. De Wolf's private office furnishing a temporary shelter. The last case, which came up yesterday, was from the Chicago House, a cheap lodging-place on Clark street. How long the public is to be annoyed in this way is one of the unanswered questions. There is one thing certain, some other temporary place of shelter should be provided for homeless small-pox unfortunates.

Boston, Dec. 3.—Weeks has made a proposition to the Examiner of the Pacific Bank, which has been referred to the Controller, and upon his reply depends the future of the bank.

NEWARK, N. J., Dec. 3.—It is reported that arrangements will be made to relieve the creditors of the Mechanics' National Bank by partial payment, and to revive the bank.

AN ALABAMA RIOT.

Two Negroes Killed by Officers of the Law.

Jacksonville (Ill.) Republican.

Last Saturday, as usual on that day in Anniston, several hundred negroes and white men gathered there. It seems there was more than the usual amount of drinking done that day by the negroes, and early in the morning quite a body of them evinced a riotous disposition.

About 12 o'clock the Marshal had occasion to arrest a negro whom no had been ordered to bring before H. L. Jeffers, Esq., for carrying concealed weapons. When the arrest was made, the negroes assumed such a threatening attitude that the Marshal was compelled to strike one with a club to keep the crowd off him. After trial this man was incarcerated in the calaboose until arrangements could be made for sending him to jail. Subsequently the Marshal arrested another negro, and started with him to the calaboose. He was followed again and closely pressed by a howling, profane gang of negroes who were urging the prisoner not to suffer himself to be incarcerated.

They pressed around and about the Marshal and his deputy from the place of arrest to the calaboose, and by the time of his arrival there they pressed him so closely he did not have time to unlock the prison door. At this juncture a white man named Mulke pressed forward and took the keys. The Marshal faced the crowd, and, drawing his pistol, ordered them to stand back or he would fire.

At this juncture Greenwood, the leader of the rioters, sprang forward and struck the Marshal with a rock, making a rather severe wound on the head and nearly bringing him to the ground. The Marshal fired upon him at once and shot him down. At the same instant the Deputy Marshal (Smith) opened fire on the rioters, and the prisoner (Hammond) who was making his way to where the Marshal and Greenwood were engaged, was shot, and, running up a flight of several steps, fell. There were four shots fired and two negroes shot, one of whom died instantly and the other the following Monday morning.

The Justice of the Peace, Mr. Jeffers, held an inquest over the body of Hammond and subsequently that of Greenwood, the verdict of the jury being in the latter case that he came to his death at the hands of officers of the law while in the lawful discharge of their duty.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES
Thomas Garfield, an Uncle of the President, Killed by the Cars--A Party of Lynchers in Michigan Foiled by the Sheriff's Wife--Great Destruction of Grain, Farm Houses and Machinery by Fire in California--The Daily Record.

FOILED BY A PLUCKY WOMAN.

DETROIT, June 22.—A second attempt was made at an early hour this morning to reach and lynch Waskamp, lying in jail at Grand Haven, who shot his employer, Lyman Cady, about a month ago at Lamont. Some dozen of the most respected farmers of that vicinity suddenly appeared at the jail at the hour named, overpowered the deputy sheriff and compelled him to give them the keys to the murderer's cell. They then all went in and secured their victim. The sheriff's wife, aroused by the noise, in the absence of her husband from town, went to the spot, discovered the situation, closed the outside door of the jail, which the lynching party had left unguarded, and bagged the whole lot. She then sent a servant girl to ring the fire alarm, which called out the citizens and completely frustrated the attempt.

SHOOTING AFFRAY.

COUNCIL BLUFFS, June 22.—Between three and four this afternoon a fatal shooting affray occurred in the office of the Ogden hotel, in which Harry McGee, head waiter at the Pacific hotel, shot and instantly killed Geo. Washington, waiter at the Ogden house. Both were colored. McGee followed Washington into the hotel after having a scuffle with him outside, and, drawing a revolver, deliberately fired, the ball taking effect in or close to his heart, from which Washington died in a moment or two. McGee was arrested. The trouble originated over a colored woman with whom both were in love. Yesterday McGee hunted for Washington and threatened then to kill him.
STRUCK BY AN ENGINE.
BROCTON, Mass., June 22.—As the 8 o'clock train from Fall River approached Huntington Heights station a hack driven by Mr. Early was struck by the engine, demolishing it. Early was thrown twenty-five feet and killed, and the two occupants of the carriage, James Bennett and J. Shields, were terribly injured, probably fatally. Both horses were killed.

DROWNED.
CHICAGO, June 22.—Samuel Randall, a hostler, and Hall, a colored man, drove into the river this forenoon to wash a buggy, when by some means the horses and men were drowned and the buggy was carried down the stream.

THROUGH A BRIDGE.
FREEPORT, Pa., June 22.—A serious accident occurred here between 4 and 5 o'clock this afternoon. The west bound freight train on the Pennsylvania road ran over a cow near the Buffalo creek bridge, throwing the engine off the track on the bridge, causing the bridge to fall, and precipitating the engine and ten cars into the creek. The engineer, Jas. E. Repine, and the fireman, Jas. Delrich, were both killed. Major Snowden, of Freeport, a passenger, was also killed. The bodies have since been recovered. That of the engineer, was found wedged in the timbers. A brakeman named Gallagher made a narrow escape by jumping off a box car. Repine and Delrich lived at Blaisville, Pa.

BRUTAL DEED.
LITTLE Rock, June 22.—A Gazette specia says a brutal crime occured near Luckanwork day before yesterday, when H. Parnell, aged 60 years of age, raped a little daughter, aged 7, of Maurice Crabb. Parnell had been in the employ of Mr. Crabb as a farm hand some time, and had been received in the father's family. The little girl had been in the habit of carrying out fresh water to the field where the men were at work. Mr. Crabb had occasion to go to the house a short time. Mr. Crabb returned again, and was surprised to find the old man in the act of accomplishing his dreadful purpose. Parnell, on seeing he was detected, ran away, and Mr. Crabb, after caring for the child, gave the alarm to his neighbors. Great indignation prevails, and a large number of citizens went in pursuit. The old man was finally captured in the evening, about four miles from the scene, in a thick wood. Yesterday morning, on being taken before the justice of Jackson, he pleaded guilty to the charge of rape, and was remanded to jail.

GRAIN FIRE.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 22.—A dispatch from Merced, says to-day fires swept over some 7,250 acres of wheat and other grain, destroying everything in its course, including many farm houses and much farming machinery. Loss not known.

AN UNCLE OF THE PRESIDENT KILLED.

CLEVELAND, O., June 22.—Shortly after 3 o'clock this afternoon, the east bound train on the New York, Pennsylvania & Ohio railway, when about twelve miles from here, struck a buggy, in which were riding Thos. Garfield, uncle of President Garfield, and Mrs. Alonzo Arnold, sister of Dr. Boyton, cousin of the President. Thomas Garfield was instantly killed, and Mrs. Arnold's skull so badly fractured life is despaired of. The buggy was dragged about 200 feet before the train stopped. Mr. Garfield was eighty years old. He leaves several children. Gen. Garfield and Dr. Boyton were telegraphed to at Long Branch.

POISONED.

ATLANTA, Ga., June 22.—At a picnic at Decatur thirty-five people were poisoned by eating chicken salad. The chicken had been boiled in a brass kettle. All suffered severely, but no serious consequences resulted.

Before the New York Bribery Investigation Committee John I. Davenport was sworn. He said he saw Senator Strahan's statement in the papers. As it reflected on President Garffeld and himself, he obtained the former's permission to state what had taken place between them, and made a similar request of Postmaster-General James and Mr. Knox. Went to the White House in May with the Postmaster-General. The President asked witness who would be a good man for the Marshalship. Witness replied that he did'nt know, and the President suggested Mr. Knox. Witness said the appointment would be an excellent one, and at Garfield's request had a long talk with Knox about the place. Knox insisted that he did not want it, as he was unacquainted with the politicians and was afraid it would interfere with his professional business. Finding him unwilling to accept, Judge Gardner's and Ehard's names were again brought up, followed by witness suggesting Senator Strahan. Returned to the White House, and told Garfield of Knox's refusal, and suggested Strahan. The President did not know him. Witness then telegraphed to Strahan and met him at the Union League Club that night, when witness asked Strahan about accepting the Marshalship. He told him he would be expected to vote against Conkling and Platt. Strahan asked if the offer could not be held over until after a settlement of the United States Senatorship. Witness replied "No," and Strahan promised to consider the matter. In the morning he telegraphed to witness declining the place.

Brady, through his counsel, has made application before the Court, Judge Cox presiding, for an immediate investigation by the Grand Jury of the Star Route charges. It was stated on behalf of Brady that he had been subjected to bitter assaults from the press for a long time, and he claimed the privilege of a prompt and speedy trial.

A dispatch from Tunis says the Bey's steward has taken refuge at the English Consulate with the securities and jewels which the Bey claims, together with a million francs that he embezzled as the reward of his stewardship for many years. Surprise is felt at the British Consul for protecting the embezzler.

Two negroes imprisoned on charges of outraging a white woman were taken from the jail at Danbury, N. C., by a body of armed men and hanged. The punishment is generally approved by both white and colored people.

A little girl seven years old was outraged by an old man of sixty, named Purnell, near Tuckerman, Ark. The man was lodged in jail under a heavy guard. The girl is in a critical condition.

A private telegram received at St. Louis says that C. P. Huntington, of the Southern Pacific and other railroads, has secured the controlling interest in the Houston and Texas Central Railroad.

It is stated that until the relations between France and Italy become more satisfactory, the difficulties attending any attempt to place the Italian loan

on the Paris market will be practically insurmountable. France will only consent to a loan being dealt with on the Paris Bourse on condition that Italy formally withdraws her disapproval of the French policy in Tunis.

Cooper Union: New York city was crowded Thursday night with the workingmen, sympathizing with the strike of the brewery men. Sixty Trades Unions were represented. Victor Drury, the Chairman, stated that the employing brewers made a pool amounting to $80,000 or $90,000 to influence the malt dealers in the West to Boycott brewers who send beer to New York. The resolutions adopted by the meeting inasmuch as the boss brewers have proved regardless of all considerations and inapproachable by every argument. that Boycotting is the duty of every honorable citizen, as the only means left to force them to respect the rights of the workingmen.

Two simultaneous dispatches were received at Rochester, N. Y., by Prof. Swift, of the Warner Observatory, by which it appears that another great comet has been discovered.

A storm in Mayfield, Ky., leveled barus, fences and several business houses, and entirely destroyed two houses in town.

A meeting of the Cabinet has been held at Long Branch, which is now the Seat of Government.

A cyclone in the district of Blois, France, caused damage amounting to several million francs.

Suspended dividends of the Western Union Telegraph stock, amounting to three per cent, cash, will be paid July 1st.

Since the recent Prohibition Law in Kansas, "jug trains" run from Topeka to Kansas City, Mo., every Sunday, by which tipplers can go and replenish their jugs of whisky once a week. An express agent says that express shipments of whisky from Kansas City to Topeka alone average $300 worth every day.

A Chinaman who died in Boston had a Christian funeral, the services being conducted in church by a Methodist clergyman, and interpreted to the hundred or more Chinamen present by one of their countrymen. The remains were not shipped to China.

The straight Greenbackers in Maine will hold a Convention at Lewiston on the 3d of August.

Speaker A. O. Bacon is of the opinion that the Legislature can get through with its work in forty days, if not sooner.

Hon. Welborn Price, of Oconee, favors early and late sessions of the General Assembly, and a rest during the hot part of the day. He suggests a morning session from 8 to 12 o'clock, and an evening session from 4:30 to 7 o'clock. This would give ample working hours in the coolest part of the day, and expedite the transaction of business.

Col. William M. Wadley, President of the Central Railroad, reached Columbus on Wednesday morning in a special car, and left at 5 o'clock in the afternoon for Troy. Ala.

Col. J. E Jones, at the Central Georgia Bank, Macon, is engaged in issuing the $32.50 scrip dividends due upon the Southwestern Railroad stock.

Fine rains visited Burke county last week, and the farming outlook has materially brightened thereby. Farmers wear a more cheerful look.

The crops, of all kinds, in Cobb county are better than they have been in thirty years.

A horrible tale of ravishment and mutilation is related by the Chattanooga Times as having occurred on Missionary Ridge a few days ago, perpetrated upon the person of Miss Nancy Donaldson, 17 years of age, by a mulatto demon named Henry Lawson, who had a wife and five children. The young lady was also horribly mutilated with a razor, which the villain used to cut, disfigure and terrify her whenever she screamed. He was pursued, captured and imprisoned to await trial.

It is announced that Rev. S. P. Callaway, editor and proprietor of the State Line Press, at West Point, has bought the LaGrange Reporter.

The Walton Vidette says: "Among the numerous questions for consideration by the Legislature is a bill which will probably be presented, to make from the Blue Ridge and the Western Circuits a new Judicial Circuit. This is the largest circuit in the State, having eleven counties and a population of 124,000 souls. Few men are physically able to hear and decide the business of so many people in fifty-two weeks."

With the convict question, the Railroad Commissioners, the Lunatic Asylum, the temperance question, the fence question, the State capitol, the new circuit and a host of local measures, the Legislature is likely to need all the time allowed for the session.

There has been a great deal of sickness in Campbell county for the past week or two. The health of that community is improving, however, as most of those who were complaining have recovered.
