CHATTANOOGA TENN., July 11.—A well known physician of this city, Dr. Jas. E. Baily, shot and probably mortally wounded Charles Marsh, a carpenter. They are neighbors and their wives quarreled about some trivial matter. This the husbands took up, which resulted in their mortal combat to-day.

A negro name Hugh Lawson, who raped a young lady last week and mutilated her body in a most fiendish manner, has been arrested and lodged in jail. There is great danger of his being lynched. A mob of men congregated in front of the jail last night with that purpose in view, but were deterred by a strong sheriff's guard. Excitement is still high, however.

LITTLE ROCK, ARK., July 11.—Sunday morning Frank Conway, lessee of the Johnson plantation, twelve miles from this place, was shot and dangerously wounded by one of his workmen, named Walters, with whom he was quarrelling. Conway is widely known, being a nephew of ex Gov. Conway; of this city.

CINCINNATI, July 11—The United States signal service themometer here registered 103.5 at 3:15 yesterday afternoon. Ordinary thermometers registered from 7 to 8 degrees higher in the shade. The heat was the greatest on record here. This coroner was called to attend thirteen deaths, all from congestion of the brain, supposed to have been superinduced by the excessive heat. There were twelve sunstrokes, though no fatal cases were reported up to midnight. In Covington, Ky., there were six cases of sunstroke yesterday, four of them fatal.

CANTON, Miss., July 11.—From reliable information received and dispatches seen Neshoba county, on Saturday, instructed for Major Barksdale for Governor. Forty-five delegates, out of fifty-two, in Lowndes county are for Stone for Governor, and in Lincoln county forty out of fifty country delegates are for J. M. Stone for Governor, Gwin for auditor, and Myers for secretary of state.

HOUSTON, TEXAS, July 11.—Justice Brashear has been engaged all day in the examination of the case of Bob White, colored, and W. H. Cowhart, suspected of having murdered W. H. Gleason, about two days ago. Gleason was found floating in the Bayou with his head cut off, his bowels removed and otherwise mutilated. The body was naked and had a piece cut from the breast, another from the arm and another from the leg. It was reported to-day that Gleason had his name tattooed on his body with India ink just where these cuts were made, and that the white man Cowhart knew of them. There was other strong circumstancial evidence pointing to Cowhart as the murderer.

FREDERICKSBURG, VA., July 11.—Silas Massey (colored) was shot in the breast and instantly killed on Saturday, near Acqua creek, Stafford county, by Capt. S. S. Lee. Massey was unmercifully beating a white woman, his paramour, with a heavy stick, threatening to kill her, when Capt. Lee commanded him to desist. The negro then assailed Capt. Lee with great violence, and in trying to protect himself the fatal wound was inflicted by Capt. Lee. An inquest was held by a jury, composed of white and colored men, which rendered a verdict that the killing was done in self-defense.

A DOUBLE TRAGEDY.
Murder and Masked Lynchers at Ivanpak.
On Tuesday or Wednesday of last week, in Ivanpah, Indian Winn threw a squaw into a well for some unknown cause, the squaw getting out with some slight bruises. Being afraid that the whites would kill him, Winn thought he would go down to Kestler's ranch and kill Kestler for some old grudge and go to the happy hunting grounds on the square, like a good Indian. He accordingly went to Kestler's, and finding him at home, shot him at first in the back, the ball penetrating the heart. This must have killed him instantly. He then shot him in the right breast twice, twice in the neck and once in the eye. He then carried the body into Kestler's cabin and looked the door, and two other Indians who were with him when the shooting was done, went up to Ivanpah and told the whites and Indians of the affair. The latter went down to the cabin, caught him, tied him and took him to Ivanpah. Hiram Clark and Brookfield went down to Kestler's to verify the Indians' story, and found
The Indians had taken Winn to Mr. Clark's saloon, and late in the evening while a number of miners were there talking, smoking and drinking by turns, four masked men entered the place, ordered the crowd to stand back, took Winn out and hung him to a butcher's gallows near by. The crowd in the meanwhile thought they'd find out what had become of him; they soon found him hung as above stated, with one of the masked men standing guard over the body and the other three digging a grave. The guard ordered the crowd to "take a walk" which they did, back to the saloon, standing not upon the order of their going.

Winn confessed to the killing of three other white men before Kestler, said he killed him for fun; he said he had killed four Indians, one his own child, which he brained. The Indians would have hanged him themselves but were afraid of the whites interfering. He was well known hereabouts, spoke good English, and was hard to beat in a polite game.—Sus Bernording

A MURDERER'S CONFESSION. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. LEAVENWOIRR, Ks., March 29.—The devilish details of the murder of Henry Ketchell, a German living alone on a claim near Cawker City, as hitherto wired, are now fully corroborated. R. W. Know, his son Charles, L. M., Soule, and Theodore Kinyon were arrested for the crime, and the latter has just made a confession that the four went to Ketchell's dugout and dropped an iron thimble filled with powder down into the stove. After the explosion, when Ketchell rushed from the cablin, he was fired at as he emerged, was pursued, and again fired on, and after a terrible struggle for his life, in which he was beaten over the head with a gun barrel repeatedly, he fell to the earth and was pounded until the flonds were convinced that their bloody work was only too well done. ILLEGAL FEES.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

TORNIO, O., March 29.—Considerable excitement was caused in legal circles to-day by the arrest of J. M. Brown, a prominent attorney of this city, on a warrant issued by J. M. Bloomer, Police Prosecutor. The charge was demanding illegal fees—namely, $250 for services as Police Prosecutor for a few days last spring, when the proper amount would have been about $37. The arrest grows out of a case in the Police Court a year ago, when J. M. Bloomer, Police Prosecutor, was arrested and tried for visiting the rooms of Mrs. Stewart for improper purposes, Mrs. Stewart being also tried for keeping a house of ill-repute. Mr. Brown was employed by the city to prosecute the case.

CRIMINALS RELEASED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

TERRE HAUTE, Ind., March 29.—This afternoon the noted criminals George Jackman and James Knight, for some reason not known, were released from custody. These men were tried for throwing a train from the track of the Indianapolis & St. Louis Railroad at St. Mary's Station in June, 1870, whereby a brakeman was killed. After an exciting trial, lasting eleven days, they were sentenced to life imprisonment. The case went to the Supromo Court, judgment was reversed, and the prisoners remanded for a new trial. This afternoon they were released upon their own recognizance, which virtually ensued the matter.

A SAILOR MURDERED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

NEW ORLEANS, La., March 29.—Last Friday night a sailor boarding-house at Bull's Head was burned down, and Charles O'Brien, Mate of the ship Orlont, was supposed to have perished in the flames. To-day the testimony of one of his comrades was obtained that O'Brien had been brutally beaten and his skull fractured by a barkeeper named Goetz, and he was put to bed drunk, bleeding, and insensible. After the house was discovered to be on fire efforts were made to arouse him, and he was found to be dead. Goetz was arrested to-day for the murder.

FOUND GUILTY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Boston, March 29.—Dr. Nathan Ganz, the Socialist leader, who was the prime mover in the great watch swindle, was to-day found guilty of using the mails with intent to defraud, but a motion for a new trial was at once made. The swindle was on a gigantic scale, circulators offering valuable watches for a ridiculously small sum being freely distributed in all foreign countries, and Ganz, under the assumed name of Alexander Rodanow, pulled in a very large amount of money.

STABBING AFFRAY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

EAST SAGINAW, Mich., March 29.—James Sager, of Saginaw, was walking in Midland last evening with two women when two men, strangers, came up and assaulted Sager, cutting a gash on his head. He drew a knife and stabbed one of the men, Albert Moore, six times in the side, shoulder, and arm. Sager was arrested and lodged in jail. He claims that he did the act in self-defense, and public sympathy is on his side, as Moore has a bad reputation. Moore is in a critical condition, and will probably die.

FEARS OF FOUL PLAY.
Des Moines, Ia., March 29.—Last Thursday evening Zenus W. May left his boarding-

house to go to the City Library rooms to British some business with a man whom he had just previously left there. He did not return to the Library and has not been seen or heard of since. He was known to have about $1,500 on his person. Two young men who also knew it, who were with him the evening before, disappeared Friday morning and cannot be traced.

VERDICT "NOT PROVEN."

VERDICT "NOT PROVEN."

Boston, March 29.—Alexander Rodanaw, alias Nathan Ganz, was tried in the United States District Court to-day on the charge of illegally using the mails for the purpose of swindling by bogus watches. The Government case was weak, and the Judge intimated that there was not enough evidence to convict. The case comes up again to-morrow, when it is expected Ganz will be discharged.

HANGING A REDSKIN...

Some Indians in the vicinity delivered the murderer to the authorities, but soon after a number of masked men took him out and hung him.

HORSE-THEVES.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
ELGIN, Ill., Dec. 29.—A horse, harness, cutter, and robe belonging to A. J. Hendrickson and S. W. Kingsley, living in the country east of here, was stolen from their barn last night by horse-thieves. The horse was a bay, seventeen hands high, weighed 1,150 pounds, had a film over the right eye, and a cut on the left fore heel.

A WEST VIRGINIA SHOOTING.

A WEST VIRGINIA SHOOTING.
CHARLESTON, W. Va., March 29.—A row at a dance on Campbell's Creek resulted in the fatal shooting of Henry Hancock and the serious wounding of Jim Holstein by one Clay, a workman. The workman made good his escape. Hancock is bleeding internally, and his death is hourly expected. Holstein will survive.

YOUNG FEMALE CONVICT.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
CLINTON, Ill., March 29.—Martha Borum, aged 16 years, the partner of Lizzie Barton, the female horse-thief, of this county, was sent to the Penitentiary this afternoon for one year, for arson in burning some buildings in Wapella. The jury was out twenty hours.

CAUSED BY WHISKY.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
BATTLE CREEK, Mich., March 29.—During a drunken quarrel late last night, George Arnold, a young man, fatally stabbed A. McDonald, a night-watchman at the Chicago & Grand Trunk depot.

MURDERED BY HIS PARTNER. BATAVIA, O., March 29.—Mengro news has been received of the murder of a German emilgrant by his fellow-partner at Utopia, seven miles above Felicity, on the Ohio River. Neither could speak or understand English.

A FATAL WOUND.

A FATAL WOUND.

BATAVIA, O., March 20.—In a row at Fell- lity William Dodson and Francis Williams were seriously stabbed by Frederick Seme; all colored. Dodson's wound was through the neck, and will probably prove fatal.

A NEW TRIAL WANTED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

GENEVA, Ill., March 28.—The Kane County Circuit Court resumed session to-day, and Judge Kellam is hearing the argument for a new trial in the "10omas murder case.

CUT WITH A KNIFE.

Detroit, Mich. March 29.—George Arnold had a flight with a night-watchman, A. McDunald, at Battle Creek, Mich., last night, and cut him terribly with a knife. Arnold is still at large.

KILLED BY HER BROTHER.
St. Paul, Minn., March 29.—A special says a Mrs. Cleary, of Manston Station, Wilkin County, died to-day of injuries inflicted by her brother, John Ward, in a quarrel. Ward was arrested.

Dubuque tells a horrible story of his experience during the winter. He homesteaded 160 acres at Big Lake, Dakota, two years ago, and last year harvested sixty acres of wheat, yielding twenty-five bushels per acre, for which he realized $1,200; with this he laid in a supply of fuel and fixed up his house for winter; otherwise the family would have perished. Two neighboring families, not so well fixed, came to live with them, and the three families in one house had hard work to keep from freezing. The fuel ran out and they used all the railroad ties and telegraph poles they could dig out of the snow; then the houses of the other two families were, little by little, torn down and burned, and nearly all their furniture went the same way. A German neighbor named Becker, with a five-horse team, attempted to reach the station for a supply of coal. He was caught in a snow-drift, and two days afterward he was found frozen stiff in the sleigh, his faithful dog lying on his breast, also dead. The five horses were all frozen stiff, standing upright in the drift. Becker's body was taken home to his bereaved wife and children. It was nailed in a stout box and placed in a corn-crib until it could be buried in the spring. Another family had lived some time on soup made of an ox hide.

We have before noticed this neat-looking paper, but our contemporary did not see the mention. The paper is a handsome weekly of six pages of six columns each. H. Brundage is proprietor, and J. F. Kline local editor. It is well filled with good reading matter, and contains all the news of the railroad terminus, and has a good share of advertising. We wish it success.

The Piegans and Blood Indians belonging to the British side of the line have arrived from the Judith and Musselshell country where they have been following the buffalo for two years past. They are miserably poor and say they can hunt buffalo no longer among their enemies. They go to the vicinity of Ft. McLeod, in hopes their grandmother will feed them. They promise not to kill or steal cattle on the way. Good bye to them.

A dispatch, received to-day from Fort Benton states that last night, while crossing the Marias river, the ferry boat upset, precipitating several men and two wagons into the river. Quinn, Master of transportation at Fort Assiniboine, was drowned. A teamster named Kinney floated off on a piece of ice. He was last seen at the mouth of the Marias, and said he was too weak to hold on longer. Aa no boat could be obtained to rescue him, it is supposed that he also perished.

We learn that J. N. Jones, of Meagher county, narrowly escaped lynching at Benton recently, and was only spared on his family's account and a promise to leave town in three days. It appears that he has been caught killing and skinning cattle for their hides, killing sheep dogs to have the pleasure of seeing their owners put to great trouble and inconvenience in getting others, and telling working men that their employers could not pay their wages, etc. He has probably left the country, and it will be unhealthy for him if he returns. San Pierre, a Flathead Indian, sentenced from the Second Judicial District in December, 1878, to three years' imprisonment in the Montana Penitentiary for the crime of manslaughter, died on Tuesday evening of Bright's disease of the kidneys. INDEPENDENT.

As a large number of applications for the establishment of new postoffices in Montana will be made during the coming season, we give the following instructions issued by the First Assistant Postmaster General relative to the selection of names for new postoffices: In selecting names for postoffices it is particularly desired that the name of the town or village in which the office is to be located should be adopted. if such name is in no way similar to that of any established office in the State. The prefix of East, Centre, New, North, South or West to the name of a postoffice is objectionable; as also is the addition of Burgh, Centre, City, Corners, Creek, Cross Roads, Depot, Hill, Hotel, Holland, Junction, Mill, Mound, Peak, Plains, Point, Port, Prairie, Rock, River, Run, Ridge, Store, Station, Springs, Town, Vale, Valley or Village, as such prefixes or additions lead to confusion and delay in the transmission of mails. Short names should be selected for postoffices. To insure favorable action on applications for postoffices the above instructions must be complied with.

EUFAULA, ALA, June 9.—A most villainous outrage was committed upon a respectable white girl, twelve years old, by Josh Shorter, a negro, near this city late yesterday afternoon.

A TRAIN-ROBBER SENTENCED. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Sept. 28.—Bill Ryan, one of the James boys gang, who participated in the first Glendale train-robbery on the Chicago & Alton Road in October, 1879, was today found guilty, and sentenced to the Penitentiary for twenty-five years. Ryan was convicted mainly on the testimony of Tucker Basham, an ex-convict, who was pardoned by Gov. Crittenden that he might testify in this case. Basham participated himself in the train-robbery, and was sent to the Penitentiary for ten years for the part he took in that affair, he having pleaded guilty to the charge. Basham's life was threatened last week if he dared testify against Ryan, and while on the witness stand his house near Independence was set on fire by his enemies and totally destroyed.

THE WILLIAMS BROTHERS.

THE WILLIAMS BROTHERS.

St. Louis, Sept. 28.—Several posses of men, both in Illinois and Missouri, are searching for Alonzo and Edward Maxwell, better known as the Williams brothers, who killed Sheriff Lammy, of Calhoun County, Illinois, last Sunday, and wounded one of his deputies. A detachment of St. Louis police are also in pursuit of the fugitives. Those men who were yesterday floating down the Mississippi River in a skiff, took the land today at a point in Lincoln County, and are supposed to be making across this State with a view of getting to the Indian Territory. A posse of Lincoln County men are on the trail, and eight or ten policemen and detectives of this city, said not to be far behind them, crossed the country from a point near Alton to intercept them. The belief is strong that those desperados will be captured.

JENNIE CRAMER.

NEW HAVEN, Conn., Sept. 28.—An interesting discovery was made at the Malloy trial today. On the Branford Point Hotel register was exhibited the name of Jennie Cramer Aug. 5. The counsel for the defense claimed that it must have been put there recently. King, the clerk, had never noticed it before. The record showed that Walter Malloy was there with Miss Douglass July 30. This record had been erased or rewritten under July 31. The clerk had spoken to Walter about the change. The entry showed that Walter and Miss Douglass had supper at the hotel Friday, Aug. 5. Witness today testified to seeing them on the road hither, and one witness on their return to New Haven in the evening near 10 o'clock.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Hoffman, who came from Franklin, Ind., to this city about two years ago, originally from Pennsylvania, and who has suddenly made himself a general favorit in society and professionally, was today placed in jail on the charge of forgery and obtaining money on false protenes, many persons having been victimized out of sums ranging from $20 to $100 on checks purporting to have been drawn in his favor by others, who pronounce them forgeries and drawn by himself on banks where he had no deposit. TWO MURDERERS LYNCHED.
MILWAUKEE, Sept. 28.—A special from Oconto, Wis., states that two roughs named McDonald and Cousins, who brutally murdered two brothers named Mitson near Menomineo, Mich., a few days ago, were taken from jail and lynched last night.

INDICTMENT QUASHED.
TRENTON, N. J., Sept. 28.—In the United States Court today the indictment against ex-Congressman Charles H. Voorhis for embezzlement was quashed.

OBITUARY.

R. F. RUTH.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
SPRINGFIELD, Ill., Sept. 28.—R. F. Ruth, Esq., one of Springfield's most respected and esteemed citizens, died to-day of dropsy of the heart after a comparatively brief illness. Mr. Ruth was born in Wrightsville, Pa., Aug. 26, 1815, and came to Springfield in 1839. He was engaged successfully in the saddliery and harness and then in the dry-goods business until 1875, when he engaged in the hardware business. Since 1868 he has been President of the Marine Bank.

mcdonald-oconto-1881-09-28.A17:
Murder and Lynch Law.
Frank and John McDonald, two ex-convicts who have just completed an eighteen-months' term in the State prison, and have been out only two weeks, while at a disreputable house in the outskirts of this village, day before yesterday, got into a row with Willie Kittson, a half-breed, about 23 years old. Norman Kittson and one Tommy Dunn went to the relief of Willie, and took him from the house and started for home. The McDonalds followed them and attacked them again on the street. Willie was knocked down and then stabbed several times. Norman received several severe knife wounds in the face and side. Willie died within a few moments after receiving his wounds, and Norman can not live. The McDonalds were promptly arrested by Sheriff Barclay and lodged in the county jail, where they remained until last evening. Great excitement prevailed from the time of the murder, and extra guards were placed over the jail. About 10 o'clock last night a mob of over 500 people, composed mostly of Frenchmen, Indians and half-breeds, approached the jail, overpowered the Sheriff and guard, and with heavy timbers, sledgehammers and axes broke open the door of the jail and of the cell where the McDonalds were lodged. The prisoners were pulled out of the cell and long ropes fastened about their necks, and they were then dragged by the mob mercilessly through the street for three-quarters of a mile to the house where the row originated, where their bodies were suspended to a tree. The victims were dead, however, long before their bodies were hung up. The house above mentioned was then set on fire and burned to the ground. The two bodies were left suspended to the tree until this morning, when they were taken down by the authorities. When the jail was attacked, a large number of citizens responded promptly to the call of the Sheriff for help, but the mob had obtained entrance to the jail, and resistance was then impossible.

South and West.
Wisconsin Democratic heroe
The Wisconsin Democrat have nominated a full State ticket headed by N. D. Fratt for governor.

The Minnesota Republican State convention put a full ticket in the field with L. F. Hubbard for governor at the head.

Two cousins named McDonald, who had murdered two half-breed Indians at Menominee, Mich., were taken forcibly from jail by a crowd of 500 men and killed.

The ship Alice Buck, from New York, was wrecked on the California coast and ten out of the twenty-four men on board were drowned.

A SPRINGFIELD (Ill.) dispatch says that ever since the death of President Garfield Mrs. Lincoln has been suffering the most intense mental anguish. She frantically declares that an assassin murdered her husband and will soon kill her son Robert if he continues to remain in Washington. She wants him to resign and leave public life altogether. He is her only child.

The three robbers who recently robbed the train on the Iron Mountain road, in Missouri, have been captured.

A TERRIBLE cyclone swept through the cottonwood valley, in the vicinity of Topeka, Kansas, for a distance of thirty miles long and one to four miles in width. Houses and barns were torn to pieces and trees twisted off or uprooted. Twelve persons are known to have lost their lives and a number are missing.

Presley Cowan made his first ascent in a balloon at Washington, Ohio, and a descending got entangled in trees, when he either fell or jumped out of the basket and was killed.

Charles Pierce, an imprisoned horse thief, who shot and killed Jailer Franks while the latter was conveying him from one cello another in the jail at Bloomington, Ill. was lynched by a large crowd. The dispatch says that some of the best citizens were in the front ranks of the lynchers. Leading business men cheered and encouraged the lynchers, and women waved their handkerchiefs in application. For two hours the sheriff, with all his force, the police force and other officials stood at the jail door and fought and pleaded with the infuriated crowd. Governor Cullom ordered the sheriff to call out the militia, but they could not be assembled in time.

Mrs. MARY CRAIG, the largest woman in the United States, and the wife of the so-claimed, largest man in the country, died at Danville, Ind., the other night of dropsy of the heart. She weighed over 800 pounds, and was over six feet high. She was known as Barnum's fat woman. It required six men to handle the body.

KINKADE, the best acrobat in Forepaugh's circus, missed in turning a somersault while performing at Pulaski, Tenn., struck on his head and was killed.

OBER & HAGEMAN.
John A. Anderson, the well-known broom-corn dealer, has returned from New Mexico for a short visit.

Mrs. A. A. Parkerson and Mr. and Mrs. C. A. Gundaker, of Manhattan, are spending the holidays with Mr. and Mrs. John Flagg, of this city.

Notwithstanding the closeness of the times which has prevailed here, it is the belief that more money was spent for Christmas goods than ever before.

"Thousands of the best people of Chicago have heard the Tennesseeans, and all are sure to go a second and third time." Thus saith the Chicago Evening Journal.

It is stated that Mason & Morgan's Uncle Tom's Cabin troupe, will soon give an entertainment here. They have with them a trick donkey and trained blood hounds.

We understand that Madam Scott, accompanied by her troupe, has departed for Colorado. She will star it in the provinces. Good riddance to bad, very bad rubbish.

District Court is no more. It was adjourned since die last Monday. This term will be known in history as one of the most important sessions we have ever had in Saline county.

We were in error in announcing last week that the public schools were to have a two weeks' vacation—only one week. The schools will commence again next Monday.

Rev. A. J. Hartock, pastor English Lutheran Church, will preach a sermon with reference to the opening year on next Sabbath morning. All are welcome to a seat in this beautiful sanctuary.

The late Father and Mrs. Dooney left money with which to purchase a beautiful prayer book for each Sabbath school scholar of the Episcopal Church, and the books were presented on Christmas eve.

The evenings this week are pretty well taken up with entertainments: Wednesday night, "Under the Gaslight." Thursday night, the Paige lecture. Friday and Saturday nights, the Union Spy.

The Salina Rifles as now officered, has Lewis Hanback for Captain, C. T. Hilton for First Lieutenant and Chas. Bush for Second Lieutenant. The commissions from the Governor have not yet arrived.

Provided satisfactory arrangements for the money are made, and the weather continues as favorable as it now promises, work will commence all along the line of the Topeka, Salina & Western, shortly.

On Thursday evening last a very pleasant company was gathered at the residence of Mr. and Mrs. C. S. Radcliff. This excellent couple succeeded in entertaining their guests in a most delightful manner.

Mr. G. S. Shaw and daughters, who have been residing at the farm some nine miles south of Salina, have returned to Canada, to reside there permanently. We are sorry to see these excellent people leave us.

Two things have definitely been settled upon by the Topeka, Salina & Western railroad company, and they are: 1st, That the road will positively be built to Salina. 2nd, That Salina will be the end of a division.

Mr. A. B. Maxey, from Pueblo, arrived this week, accompanied by the Misses Addie and Mattie Maxey, well known to our citizens. Miss Addie has been quite sick but is convalescent. — Council Grove Republican.
We are indebted to Bartlett & Jenkins for the present of a very fine Christmas roast of beef. These popular butchers keep the best beef the market affords, and always give their customers the best of satisfaction.

Judge Hamilton informs us that a Topeka, Salina & Western surveying party will start out from Salina in an eastward direction in about two weeks, and that the right of way matter will be worked up about the same time.

ASSARIA, Ks., Dec. 27, 1881.

ED. JOURNAL—When is the lawful time to kill quail? Please answer in the JOURNAL.

Between the first days of November and January.

The bastile of Fifth street has fallen. With it has gone down many hopes and many fears. Those imprisoned by its vile fetters are free again—free as the prairie air. On its ruin it would be but just to erect a “temple of victory.”

The “Union Spy” entertainment is not to be given at Abilene, as was designed. This is owing to the number of entertainments—a home entertainment among the rest—which will occupy the attention and demand the ducats of the overstrained Abilineites.

An elegant gilt memorial cross—in memory of the late Father and Mrs. Dooley—has been presented to the Episcopal Church of this city by Misses Amanda and F. E. Dooley, daughters of the deceased. Subscribe for the Leader. Let every colored man who favors the elevation of his race subscribe for the Leader; and let every white man who believes that slavery was a crime against humanity and that it is the duty of the ruling race to aid the Negro in his struggle for moral, social and intellectual elevation do likewise.
A GREAT deal has been said about the superior school advantages enjoyed by the colored people in some of the southern states which have been under Democratic control. An itelligent colored gentleman who has traveled extensively in the South informs us that these stories are not only rose colored but iu most cases absolutely false. In the larger cities the schools are very good but in most of the smaller places and in the country they are as a rule worthless. In many communities in the country, said he, competency is a positive disqualification for a teacher.

The school authorities do not want thoroughly qualified teachers for the colored schools. When such apply, they will not employ them. Some idea of the inducements held out to competent teachers may be drawn from the fact that in Alabama the average salary of teachers is twenty-three dollars per month. There is, possibly, one consolation in this, said our informant, for if by any mishap we get hold of a competent teacher, we've got him for all time, for he can never get money enough to get away. All these things go to show that the liberal movement in the South has come none too soon, and that the salvation of the South depends upon its success.

With all the encouragement and facilities the State and community can give, the poverty and inexperience of the colored people will still form obstacles in the way of intellectual advancement, than which no people ever had to meet greater. No community can afford to foster ignorance. Sooner or later a better harvest must be reaped. The Southern whites will bless the colored people not more than themselves by consecrating their influence their energy and their means to the great work of educating and elevating the masses.

THE Atlanta Cotton Exchange which has just closed is doubtless the greatest Industrial achievement of the South since the war. It was a magnificent exposition of the products of American genius and American labor. It was also a grand exponent of the New South that is to be. The success of this Exposition is an indication that the eyes of Southern men are being opened to the folly of the past and that they are, at last, turning their backs upon the brutish suicidal policy which for fifteen years has driven out and excluded Northern capital and made a social pandemonium of the fairest section of our country. Murder, assassination, and every species of brutality and crime became the common heritage of nearly every Southern community. The poor were made poorer and every real interest of the people was sacrificed to the passions, preduices and base ambitions of a few unworthy leaders, and the bummer element which the Confederate army turned loose.

At last reason has returned and the people see that no community that wrongs and persecutes any class of citizens can hope to gather the golden fruits of prosperity and happiness.

Northern capital is now not only being welcomed but invited and solicited by the south. And in every State in the South liberal parties are springing up, with material development and fair treatment of the colored people as the cardinal principles of their faith. The exposition though a southern institution was in a large measure the product of Northern brain, Northern industry and Northern capital. It brought together crowds of men from every section of the country. It cannot help but have an excellent influence in teaching the young, men of the South, black and white, the possibilities and the dignity of free labor.

The current number of the Century Magazine contains an excellent article on the "Significant aspects of the Atlanta Cotton Exchange" in which some very interesting facts are stated.

Leather was on exhibition from the tannery at Chattanooga Tennessee, the largest single tannery in the country, and worked entirely by colored men.

A grandson of John C. Calhoun said: "If my grandfather and his associates had known as much about the Negro as I know, and could have had the same faith in his capacity for progress which I have attained from my own experience, there would have been neither slavery nor war."

We cannot better close this article than by quoting the following eloquent paragraph from the article referred to:

"But the clouds in the sky are beginning to clear away. The country is taking on settled habits, The planter has become more industrious and economical; the Negro who emerged from slavery without a dollar and with no experience of providing for himself, has by industry in many instances been able to buy mules, wagons, farming implements, cattle, etc., and thus to surround himself with the comforts of a home. Many others have enough to support themselves for one year. In spite of everything, many have prospered. The fertility of the soil and their own industry have been in their favor. And here permit me to digress far enough to say that I believe if our ancestors could have foreseen the present condition of the Negro, there would have been no war."

The Interior Dep't has 1,601 employes, of which 113 are colored.

Peter H. Clark delivered a lecture Sunday at Turner Hall, Cincinnati, on "Tom Paine."

The Washington Item fears that the Republican party by its inconsistency will alienate the colored vote.

Clara Louise Kellogg and Hon. E. D. Bassett, formerly minister to Hayti, were classmates, says the People's Advocate.

A scheme is on foot to get 1,500 colored people from Kentucky and Southern Illinois to emigrate to Colorado in the Spring.

Of the 600 convicts in the Arkansas penitentiary, 100 are bloody murderers. Six-eighths of the whole number are colored.

J. O. Lewis, colored, merchant tailor in Boston, does a $50,000 business per annum. This is decidedly a better showing than politics or law.

What's the world coming to? Two white men have been arrested; crime, murder of Rev. Marshall Smith, colored, at Clinton, La.

Mrs. Lewis C. Andrews, of Chicago is 103 years old. Born in the West Indies and witnessed the inauguration of George Washington.

The natives of Central Africa speak forty different languages, but all get there one way in eating the good missionary. We starve him to death in this country.

John Shafer, 32 years of age, of James-town Dakota Ter., is the owner of a dry good store and barber shop in said town. He is said to be worth $100,000. He is of Tiffin Ohio.

"We is gittin mo like de white trash ebery day." The colored Baptist Sunday school, of Springfield Mo., has an orchestra of four pieces to play during the services.

West Virginia colored people wish to raise $15,000 to endow the John Brown Professorship in Storer College. The money, would do more good if given to John Browns poor, old and suffering widow.

The colored Republicans, South, complain that they are not counted, in the distribution of offices. It is ever thus. In the words of the Conservator, "We deserve ten thausand more offices than we get," and it might be added than "we will get."

Mrs. Coppin, better known as Miss Fannie Jackson, delivered a lecture at Washington, lately, on Labor. She presented the importance of mechanical and agricultural labor as forming the basis of a nation's progress and power instead of professional pursuits. That kind of argument has the solid ring.

mrs-scott-salina-1881-12-27.A3:
INFAMOUS.
Judge Lynch Badly Needed.

We clip from the Denver Star the following account of an outrage perpetrated on three helpless colored women, at Salina Kansas, which for its supreme deviltry cannot be excelled in the annals of crime. If such acts of violence can happen in "free Kansas" and the perpetrators goe unpunished, then the good citizens of the state should take law in their own hands and mete out to the villains their deserts.

"We promised in our last issue to give some particulars of, and make some comments on the disgraceful outrage committed on the family of a Mrs. Scott, a colored lady of Salina, Kansas, who, with her three daughters, have sought an asylum in Denver. Had the cuticle of Mrs. Scott's skin been white, the two scoundrels who degraded and laid waste her home, would have been lynched; but no, she is a poor Negro, and must submit to all the indignities cast upon her by the despisers of her race, as if the devil had made one and God the other. The facts of Mrs. Scott's case are these: This lady's two daughters, just entering into the ages of womanhood, had gained the affection of two white men, and were by them seduced. They are said to be prominent citizens of Salina. The mother of the unfortunate girls was ignorant of their intimacy with these rogues, until they proved to be enciente, when they could no longer keep this as a secret from their parent, and they accordingly revealed to her their sad condition, and gave up the authors of their betrayal. As is natural with all fond parents, Mrs. Scott became indignant, and threatened to prosecute the despoilers of her daughters' chasity, which only tended to arouse the ire of the two men, who were led to resort to some extraordinary measures to hush up this disgraceful matter. Finding the stratagem impossible, they there upon threatened the whole family with bodily injury if they did not leave the town at once—thus assuming the position of the Czar of Russia. Mrs. Scott refused to leave, and commenced to make arrangements to institute proceedings for damages. Matters promising to assume a most disagreeable aspect for the two scoundrels, they offered to pay Mrs. Scott liberally if she would drop the matter, and keep silent; but this noble-hearted woman determining to avenge the wrong done her offsprings, refused to accept any compromise. This made confusion worse confounded, for on the night of the 27th of December, a mob surrounded this lady's house, set fire to it, and ordered her to take her daughters and leave town. The house being completely destroyed and the unfortunate family left houseless, fearing at the same time that no protection would be afforded them by the authorities, they had no other alternative but to consent to a proposition of accepting tickets and hurry away to Denver, where they now are. Although the Salina Herald denounced this infamous act of arson, and demanded that the perpetrators be sought out and punished, the authorities have been lukewarm in the matter, and no attempt has been made to discover and bring to justice the perpetrators of this diabolical act.

Now, we are living in an age of civilization, and in a country where the laws ought to be dealt out to all, irrespective of creed, color, or position; and we cannot see why this outraged family should be so treated by the law officers of Salina. Had this occurred in free and enlightened England the guilty parties would have been ferreted out long ago and kept in durance, un il arraigned before a tribunal of justice, where they would receive the just reward of their crime. We call upon the law officers to exert themselves on behalf of this injured family, the only head and front of whose offending is the cuticle of their skin. The vox populi is the vox Dei, and on behalf of a Christian people we ask that justice be met out to the unfortunate strangers who have been compelled to make Denver their Asylum. We understand that Mrs. Scott has put the matter into the hands of an attorney, in order to bring suits against the Salina authorities for damages sustained by the burning of her house, and the two vagabonds, for having betrayed her daughters. The poor girls have been victimized by two ruthless men, whose actions bring them below the level of the brute. Is there anything more outrageous in the history of a Christian people? This is a double-handed crime, which should be met with the most condign punishment. Why should this poor colored family be singled out by these Negro-haters, to be sacrificed not only in a pecuniary point of view, but in all the social relations of life? These unfortunate girls were living quietly and respectably with their parent in her own humble cottage, paid for with her own means, the saving perhaps of years of hard toiling; and they were looked upon as idols of a mother's affection and the hope of her future joy. To be torn away by wretches, who are no better than Guiteau the assassin, and betrayed in the manner described, is aggravating in the extreme, and calls forth the indignation of every colored man and woman, who now cry aloud for vengeance against these seducers. It behooves us all to look on these poor girls with sympathy and pity, and not with derision and contempt. They are young and weak, and were at the mercy and bidding of the two fiends. They deserve the consideration of a generous-minded and sympathizing public, who we have no doubt will aid them in their present misfortune. We are however watching closely the movements in this case, and see whether this colored family will receive the same redress at the hands of the law, as their white brethren.

There are several gentleman here who are willing to assist Mrs. Scott pecuniarily in carrying through a prosecution."

While resisting the seizure of the Ivan-pah Mining company's mill at San Bernardino, Cal., John McFarlane was killed by Deputy Marshal Hesson.

Mr. Chillas, a farmer living at Brenham, Texas, protested against his son's driving over a growing crop, when the young man killed his father at one fell blow.

A bill has been passed by the Michigan house providing a fine of $1,000 and imprisonment for a year for those who publish accounts of rape, incest, seduction, murder, or executions.

A DASTARDLY attempt to blind Mrs. Frank Mordaunt, wife of a well-known actor, with Cayenne pepper, was made by a man in Brooklyn. A police officer named Campbell has been arrested for the crime.

The revenue collector at Atlanta, Ga., reports that the jails of Fauinin and Pickns counties were emptied of moonshiners by armed mobs. Commissioner Baum has given orders to have warrants issued for the arrest of the rescuing parties and see that they are hunted down.

A special agent of the treasury department captured Frank Davis, a noted counterfeiter, at Hamburg, Iowa. On his person were found bogus coins of a high order of merit, and a large chunk of metal.

Three officers have reached St. Louis with Myers, Brown, and Mitchell, the Sikeston deperadoes. Sheriff Walters eluded lynching parties at New Madrid and took his prisoners to Cairo by steamer.

A Kentucky court has issued an injunction which effectually stops the business of the concern known as the Kentucky State Lottery, and which has been a very successful affair.

ABRAHAM SELLEMS was arrested in New York city, charged with forging a check for $6,000 on the Nassau bank. He confessed the crime, claiming to have lost the amount of the check in stock speculations.

PAYMASTER SWASEY, of the Cincinnati Southern road, has been asked to resign for engaging in a usurious scheme with a city jeweler. The employees of the road obtained advances of $7,000 from the jeweler last month, and gave orders on the paymaster, who shared in the profits.

It is believed that the liabilities of Robert A. Baker, the Fond du Lac banker, will reach $200,000. The tugitive has sent back $150 to apply on his default in the cemetery fund. A warrant has been obtained for the arrest of the cashier of the exploded concern, John S. Burrows, but he has fled.

REVENUE OFFICERS GARY and Looper of South Carolina, are just the kind of men for revenue officers in such a state. They set forth to seize an illicit distillery in Pickens county recently, and in doing it, notwithstanding the persons who operated it, named Alexander, father and son, resisted with shotguns. Young Alexander was seriously, perhaps fatally, wounded. The officers then destroyed an eighty-six-gallon still and about 1,700 gallons of mash and beer.

The youngest daughter—aged sixteen—of James Westover, living at Markesan, Green Lake county, Wis., died, Thursday, from taking poison—baking powder, iodine and strychnine. Her youthful lover, Dan Murray, driver on the stage route between Markesan and Brandon, and only about eighteen years old, attempted to follow by taking strychnine, but was alive when last heard from. The deluded lovers were tired of this life because Westover refused to allow Murray to call on his daughter at her home.
myers-new-madrid-1881-06.A3:
A Man Hunt.
Four counties in southeast Missouri have been deeply agitated over a man hunt. The recent slaughter of a deputy sheriff at Sikeston caused the citizens to undertake the extirpation of four desperadoes named Frank Brown, Jesse Myers, James Hamilton and Patrick Rhoades. The latter was found at a farm-house, badly wounded, and sent back under guard, but never reached Sikeston. In a fight with the others near Greenville, Sheriff Davis and J. F. Hatton were badly wounded, and one thousand armed men turned out. Near Piedmont, Hamilton was killed and Myers captured. Brown subsequently surrendered himself. The captured men were afterward hung by a mob.

MADRID BEND ITEMS.
MADRID BEND, KY.
MADRID BEND, KY.,
May 24th, 1881. }
Ed. Continuing I have contemplated write-

Ed. Courier:—I have contemplated writing you for some time, but have neglected to do so. The Courier is ever a welcome visitor, and it is with regret that we learn of your contemplated retirement from its control.

The Bend is quiet. There is not a more peaceable neighborhood in the State. Each one is pursuing the even tenor of his way. Farmers are busy, trying to regain the time lost during the last wet spell of weather. Corn looks well, tho' it is a little later than usual. There is a general complaint of a "bad stand," caused, it is supposed, by the germ being killed by the cold weather of last winter.

Col. R. C. Everett, who is, perhaps, the largest practical farmer in the bend, has 600 acres of corn which looks beautiful. It has been plowed once, and a portion of it, twice.

The prospect for wheat is very flattering. Several heads that I have examined have three and four grains to the mesh. The army worm has made its appearance in some of the wheat-fields, but not in sufficient numbers to cause any alarm.

Our New Madrid neighbors have been greatly excited over the discovery, pursuit and capture of a band of outlaws in that vicinity. The last two of the gang were captured in Wayne county, Mo., last Friday, by Capt. Lesser and an assistant. Before they were captured, they killed a man and little girl near New Madrid, and the sheriff and deputy of Wayne county. They were brought to Madrid last Sunday evening and put in jail. Shortly after dark, while Judge Lynch was organizing his court to hang them in haste and try them at leisure, the sheriff with two or three assistants took them out of jail, carried them around the town to the river, placed them in a skiff and rowed down the river about 3 miles, hailed in the Colorado, got on board and carried them to St. Louis. I hear that much indignation is expressed in consequence of the sheriff's action.

Last week, we had the pleasure of listening to an interesting lecture from Judge Kingman, on the subject of education. Think it will be productive of much good, as he succeeded in arousing the dormant interest of the people on that important subject. Respectfully, M. A. McDANIEL.
myers-new-madrid-1881-06.A6:
Capture of the New Madrid Murderers.
The following synopsis of facts we take from the New Madrid Record of the 28th. ult.: After the shooting of the Sheriff and deputy, of Wayne county, the whole population turned out to hunt the desperadoes down, and their search was rewarded next morning by the capture of all three of them. In the encounter which took place, James Hamilton was shot dead, and Jesse Myers was severely wounded. Frank Brown was taken without injury or resistance. Hamilton was burried in Wayne county. Meyers and Brown were brought back to New Madrid, and from thence, by order of Gov. Crittenden, were taken to St. Louis for safe keeping till a special term of court can be convened, when justice will be speedily meeted out to them.

The doomed outlaws slept well all of Thursdays night, and Friday morning at six o'clock received holy communion at the hands of Father Connelly. After partaking of communion, both expressed a belief that they would step from the scaffold into Heaven.

The devilish ferocity which southeast Missouri begets in her desperadoes is not more remarkable than the grim expedition with which she meets out retribution for their misdeeds. It is only two months since the New Madrid outlaws committed their first murder. To-day the gang is extinct, as Jesse Myers and Frank Brown, who have just expiated their crimes on the scaffold, were the last survivors of as precious a band of scoundrels as ever defied the law.

The story of their exploits is of blood-cusdling interest. About last Christmas Meyers, Brown, James O. Hamilton and Pat Rhodes were all living in a house near Bain's store, some nine miles from New Madrid. They had evidently at this early day banded together for mischief. Thefts occurred now and then in the vicinity and it was not long before the people began to hint that the quartette were responsible. However, there was no direct proof, and the depredations continued unchecked. Among those who were more outspoken than others, was Wm. Knox, a farmer living five miles south of New Madrid. The gang had several times threatened him but as he didn't scare they determined to make away with him. On the night of the 8th of May, they stealthily approached Knox's house. It was about 8 o'clock, dusk having fallen, but the family being still astir. Keeping well in the shadows of the shrubbery the miscreants were able to approach the house without being discovered. Then skulking under the bushes like wild beasts they watched their opportunity. There was a light in the house. Presently a man with an infant in his arms passed the window. The fatal signal was given, a volley was fired the man fell and the assassins thought their work was done.

They slunk away silently and escaped without being seen but the neighborhood had no doubt as to their identity. It so happened too that the man they had fired on was not Knox, but a visitor named Coleman. Coleman was probably saved from death by the fact that three out of the four bullets discharged struck the infant, while he himself received the fourth in the thigh. The child died in a few days.

Next day a messenger sped to New Madrid, a warrant was issued for the four men and Sheriff Walters with a posse rode out to bring them in. The miscreants were found at Bain's store, but being or

The whole country was roused in pursuit, and rewards to the amount of $2,000 were offered. Meyers, Brown and Hamilton made their way over into Wayne county. All three were skilled in woodcraft and the country is full of flat, tangled forests in which they had little difficulty in finding safety. The people in all the country around, however, were on the qui vive, and it was not written that they should escape. On the 19th of May, at evening, a travel worn stranger dropped in at Bennet's store in Greenville, the county seat of Wayne county. He was in such a tattered condition that he was taken for a tramp. His shoes were worn out and he bought a new pair which he put on. He then bought another pair, stating that his partner had gone to wake up the ferry man.

This aroused suspicion, and as soon as the man was gone the store-keeper informed Sheriff John T. Davis. Next morning Sheriff Davis and ex-Sheriff James F. Hatton started out to look for the men. They had no difficulty in tracing them to the house of a man named Lee, about a mile from town. Dismounting from their horses they quietly approached the house, being pretty well satisfied by this time that these were two of the New Madrid outlaws. The officers were well armed, but as they stepped in at the door the two men were eating breakfast and apparently at their mercy. So it did not seem that any display of weapons was necessary. Without ceremony they commanded the two to rise. The command was obeyed, but both men, who were Meyers and Hamilton, came up with a navy revolver in each hand and began to shoot without saving a word. Davis fell instantly with a bullet in his head and Hatton received a glancing wound on his skull which crazed him for the time being. He succeeded in mounting his horse and reaching town where his incoherent story created the wildest excitement. Another $2,000 reward was offered and 500 men turned out to scour the country for them. The same night, Brown, the third man, was cornered by a posse but managed to slip through their fingers somehow. Davis was at first reported dead but eventually both he and Hatton recovered.

As the news of this astounding succession of crimes spread the people of three counties wiped out their shotguns and squirrel rifles and trod the field in squads. Col. W. T. Leeper, of Mill Springs, had charge of one of the parties, his comrades being Ambrose Beatty, Cal Thomas and Taylor Fulton. Col. Leeper made up his mind that the desperadoes would try to cross Black river under cover of darkness at which is known as Campbell's switch. He accordingly posted his men and ambushed the crossings. The watchers had a weary vigil of it all night, but just as dawn was breaking two men came walking up the railroad towards the river. As the pair came along they thought at first that they were citizens scouting, but when they were quite near and were seen to be strangers of a very trampish cut the loud command was gived, "hold on there!" At the word Meyers and Hamilton, for it proved to be they, wheeled and threw up their shotguns ready to kill on the instant. But this time somebody else had the drop, and they had met some one as quick on the trigger as themselves. At the first move they made with their weapons there was a regular fusillade, and both men were cut down like weeds before a sickle. Hamilton stopped ten backshot, and Meyers was badly wounded in the head. Hamilton never moved. The ugly life was driven out of him by the leaden bullets. Neither of the bandits had fired, but both dropped with their double-barreled shotguns cocked in their hands, and each had four navy revolvers strapped upon him.

Brown, who appears to have separated from the others, was captured near Mill Springs late the same afternoon, May 21. After their flight from home the gang had formed a plan to make their way to Mexico.

Meyers and Brown, the survivors, were taken to New Madrid and safely lodged in jail, notwithstanding the high feeling against them. While there a young acquaintance of theirs named Mitchell was arrested. He was sixty miles away from all the shooting, but on hearing that his friends were in a scrape he started out to find them and give them a lift. He had no sooner began to make inquiries concerning them than he was seized and thrown into jail as an accomplice. Public excitement ran so high that the sheriff one night stealthily removed the prisoners and brought them to St. Louis for safe keeping. A special grand jury was called to indict them, and on the 14th of June, only a month after their first murder, and three weeks after they were arrested the trial was over. The jury was out twelve minutes. Judge J. D. Foster immediately sentenced Meyers and Brown to hang July 15. The odore Mitchell, for being a friend to the outlaw gang, was allowed to plead guilty to a charge of murder in the second degree and the judge sentenced him to the penitentiary for thirty years, remarking that he was the meanest of the gang.

CHICAGO, March 18.—Theodore Wolf, aged thirty six years, hung himself this morning in the attic of his house, 363 Davison street. CHARLESTON, March 18.—James Black, colored, was hanged at Marion to-day for the murder of Ell Wilcox, colored. He had been reprieved twice. As the trap fell the rope broke and Black fell heavily to the ground, spitting blood and crying for water. Eighteen minutes later the trap was spring a second time.

A Gentle Hint to Leave.

CHARLESTON, ILL., March 18.—Last night a band of masked men took out several supposed thieves and house-burners who have invested this place and committed numerous crimes lately, and string the rope and whipped them. They also warned them that more vigorous measures would be used if they do not leave.

Needs a Good Birching.

PAXTON, ILL., March 18.—Steven Morey, a boy sixteen years old, from Talbott, Indiana, took strychnine here this afternoon intending to kill himself. His condition was discovered, and his physicians think they can save his life. He says he was driven from home by the cruel treatment of his relatives, and could find no employment.

Close of a Useful Life.

ST. LOUIS, March 18.—Major John W. Booth, founder of the commission house of John W. Booth & Sons, and one of the oldest merchants of the city, died last night, aged seventy-nine years. Mr. Booth was in active business over forty years, and was well known throughout the west as a highly honorable and successful merchant.

Hid With the Hare and Hunted With the Hounds.

the Hounds.

NEW YORK, March 18.—In the prosecution of the keepers of gambling and disorderly houses, it has been ascertained, says the Tribune, that two agents of the Society for the Prevention of Crime were in the habit of giving notice of the visits of the police, so that law-breakers were enabled to defeat the end of justice.

Result of a Row in a Rum-Shop.

SAN FRANCISCO, March 18.—Jas, Adams, superintendent of the Silver Lick mine, Eureka, Nevada, and a member of the Nevada legislature, died in the city prison hospital from a pistol-shot wound received last Monday night from Adolph Schander, mailing clerk of the Evening Bulletin. The parties quarreled in a saloon about business affairs.

Destructive Fire in Newburyport.

NEWBURYPORT, Mass., March 18.—Bartlett's mills caught fire at 11 p.m. No.1 mill is destroyed, No.2 mill is on fire, and the danger threatens the Herald office and the Unifarian church. The mills corporation is fully insured. Steam船 are on the river by rail from other towns. Loss said to be very heavy.

Cost of a Customhouse.

CHICAGO, March 18.—The account of expense of building the new government custom-house and port facility shows the amount to be $8,616,000, of which the principal items are: Site, $1,250,000; stone-work and cement, $2,286,754; iron-work and hardware, $888,492; labor pay-roll, $655,006; brick, $8,758. Other less expenses make up the total.

Murdered by a Burglar.

VALLEY FORGE, PA., March 18.—Samuel Clugston, of this place, was murdered early this morning by a burglar. The latter entered the house by prying open the window, and went directly to Clugston's room, who at once seized him. In the ensuing scuffle Clugston was shot twice, and died in half an hour afterward. A man with his shirt front covered with blood has been arrested on suspicion.

Kicking Coons in Cincinnati.

CINGINNATI, March 18.—The Colored Men's Protective club at its meeting to night expressed dissatisfaction because the Republicans had given the colored men no recognition on the ticket nominated on Wednesday. They put in nomination an independent ticket containing only three of the Republican candidates, namely, police judge, clerk of the police court and a member of the board of public works.

emon Pitts, aged fifty years, was sentenced to State
prison for ten years this morning for incest with
his daughter, aged twenty. No evidence dis-
closed about disgustful condition. Of affair,

Spring Opened in Kansas.

FORT SCOTT, Kas., March 18.—Spring
opened in this locality this afternoon about 2:30
o'clock by the approach of a blistering north-
westen brigade, with it a driving snowstorm,
which continues up to this hour, 10 o'clock.
The snow is very wet, and is now about five inches
deep. At the rate which it is now falling it will
probably be a foot deep by morning.

A Kansas Tragedy.

CAWKER CITY, March 18.—Henry Kutchell, a German living alone in a dug-out, five miles
from Cawker City, was fouled murdered, an explosive being thrown in the stovepipe, which shattered the stove and demolished the house, and when Kutchell rushed out he was fired on and

fall, and was then clubbed with a gun over the head. Two parties who had had trouble with the murdered man are in jail at Deloit for the crime.

A Rough Lesson to Young Rowdies.
St. PETER, MINN. March 18.—Marshal McQuall arrested Edward O'Connor for participating in a saloon row. Twenty five or thirty of the young man's friends interfered and threw the marshal down, whereupon he pulled his pistol and fired upon the crowd, shooting the prisoner and Edward Poppin. Both were beaten and nearly fatal. They were well connected, but thoroughly trained rowdies, and deserved their fate.

And How Secretary Sekurz Had His First Intimations of Its Very Crooked Workings.

More Than a Million Acres of the Public Lande Fraudulently Sold to Innocent Purchasers.

WASHINGTON, March 18.—The investigation which led to the exposure of the alleged land swindle in Missouri, and the arrest of Robert L. Lindsay at St. Louis, and of other alleged land swindlers at Cleveland and Pittsburg, was instigated by a letter received by Secretary Schurz more than a year ago. This letter stated that Lindsay, whose father had once been in charge of the land office at Ironton, Missouri, had in his possession one or two boxes filled with United States land patents, which were certainly genuine, although Lindsay might have obtained them by questionable means. The writer of the letter alleged that Lindsay had queer dealings with queer people. Unter, who promised to be a friend to Secretary Schurz, suggested, in conclusion, that it might be well to look into the matter. The secretary secured Special-Agent D. P. Terrel, of the treasury department, to investigate the matter, and the result was the arrest of Lindsay and several other persons. It is believed at the land office that the ring have obtained fraudulent land titles to more than one million acres of public lands, most of which they have sold to innocent purchasers who, therefore, have no valid title to the land they occupy. The government officials say it rests with the secretary of the interior and attorney-general to decide whether civil suits shall be begun at once to vacate the titles

St. Louis, March 19.—The case of Ex-United States Senator D. H. Armstrong, on trial several days past for malfeasance in office while he was at the head of the police board of this city, terminated this afternoon, and the jury after a few minutes conversation rendered a verdict of not guilty.

Indicted for Attempted Assassination.

AUSTIN, MINN., March 19.—The grand jury has found an indictment against James Riley for shooting Judge Sherman Page in August last. The judge was fired upon through the widow of his study, at his home in Austin, the slugs and shot cutting his face and breast, inflicting painful but not mortal wounds.

Getting Rid of a Bad Crowd.

CHARLESTON, ILL., March 19.—Printed bills were posted all over this village last night warning some twenty persons, about half of them women, to leave the place, or be regulated by the vigilants. Several of these people were whipped a few evenings ago, as previously reported, and most of them have left town since morning. The vigilants are determined to rid the country of a gang of desperadoes and their women, who have burned houses and haystacks, have stolen cattle and horses, and robbed and plundered, and even murdered, for too years past.

A Colored "Majah" in Jeopardy.

A Colored "Majah" in Jeopardy.
CINCINNATI, March 19.—A colored man who calls himself "Major" Hicks was to-day found guilty of murder in the first degree in Covington, Kentucky, and the jury fixed the penalty at death. He is the man who brutally murdered Henry Williams at Ludlow, Kentucky, some two or three months ago. The circumstances of the murder were so cold-blooded that a determined effort was made at the time to lynch Hicks, which was only prevented by the bravery of the officers at the Covington jail. Williams was an ex-emplary young man, in the employ of the Cincinnati Southern railroad, and was killed for the purpose of robbery.

A Sanctimonious Scoundrel.

A SACRED CONSTITUTION.

WHEELING, March 19.—Quite a local sensation occurred here to-day, caused by the sudden disappearance of John H. Zevely, publisher of a whilom paper known as the Postoffice Bulletin, published semi-occasionally, and largely devoted to advertising the business of Zevely, which was that of a stencil and die cutter, mainly for use in the post-offices of the country. It was found that he has been engaged in forging in a small way for a long time past, using the names of several citizens quite freely for accommodation on banks. He had hypothecated one or two bonds isud by the Lutheran church, of which he was a member, and had forged signatures to them. He was not a man of any known bad habits, and at one time stood quite high in his church. For some time past, however, he has been regarded with suspicion. He is a ruddy-faced, boyish-looking man of about thirty-five, heavy built and is very quiet.

Revolting Case of Infanticide.

Revolting Case of Infanticide.

CINCINNATI, March 19.—"Came to its death from being stabbed by its mother. I further find that said wounds were inflicted to commit murder." The above is the verdict of the coroner this afternoon in a case of infanticide. The mother is named Matilda Streazle. The birth and infanticide occurred two weeks ago, but the discovery of the child in the privy vault was not made until last night, and then accidentally by plumbers. Twenty mortal stabs were found on its body. The mother this afternoon testified that she gave birth to the child alone in the privy, knifed it to death to still its cries, threw it into the vault to conceal her shame, but says that she was mentally deranged. She is twenty-one years old, came from Germany to Chicago a year ago, and to this city about a month ago. She and Carl Seibel, the reputed father, were arrested for murder. They came from Germany together, and are said to be cousins.

REAL ESTATE SALES.

How Values Have Gone Down Within the Past Five Years in Memphis—Valuable Property Sacrificed.

Chancery Clerk Black sold some very desirable and valuable property at remarkably low prices yesterday. The Jameson property on Front street, on south corner of the alley, north of Adams, a four-story brick storehouse on a lot 37½x148½ feet, the building having cost originally some $18,000, was sold for $7600 to W. A. Collier, who purchased it for Colonel W. A. Taylor.

The Conn property on Adams street, west of the Christian Brothers' college, lot 60x231 feet, running from Adams back to Washington street, and containing an elegant brick residence, the original cost of which was about $18,000, was sold for $7500 to Miss Edith Whittaker, a judgment creditor.

The Casten property on Mill street, Chelsea, 74½x148½ feet, containing a fine brick house built by O. H. P. Piper, contractor, was sold for $1000, Mr. Piper being the purchaser and complainant in the suit.

AMUSEMENTS.

Leubrie's Theater.

Leubrie's Theater.

Baker and Farron and supporting company closed a week's engagement at the Theater by a matinee performance yesterday, when The Emigrants was the amusing attraction. A one-play company cannot expect to draw crowded houses in Memphis, the public preferring a change of programme occasionally. Hazel Kirke is an exception, but then, it is also an exception as a dramatic attraction in every respect, yet too much of Hazel Kirke or Rip Winn Winkle palls upon the public taste. Baker and Farron will open up an engagement to-night at New Orleans.

The McCullough Engagement.

The sale of reserved seats for John McCullough's coming engagement at Leubrie's Theater begins next Thursday morning at McCarthy's, 239 Main street. The distribution of plays is as follows: Monday, Judge Conrad's tragedy, Jack Cade; Tuesday, Dr. Bird's prize t tragedy, The Gladiator; Wednesday matinee, Lady of Lyons, with Mr. McCullough as "Claude Melotte"; Wednesday night, Richard III; Thursday, farewell appearance in America, Virginius. The engagement will commence to-morrow night week, the twentieth-eighth instant.

W. C. A. Musicale.

The elegant parlors of Mr. and Mrs. S. C. Toof, 321 Linden street, will be thrown open next Tuesday evening, twenty-second instant, for the fourth social and musical of the W. C. A. in the interest of their ward visiting fund. In addition to the attractions of fine music, etc., these socials offer the best opportunity for the cultivation of that good fellowship which is a marked characteristic among the congregations of our Memphis churches, and a goodly thing to see anywhere. Our obliging amateur musicians will make this coming social one of the most delightful of the season. The invitation is general. No charges, but the usual box for free gifts for the poor.

NEWS FROM OUR NEIGHBORS.
Last week near Alexandria, Dorksb county, Tennessee, a man named Wootin shot and killed Henderson Ventres.

Dr. Atkins, of Tennessee, attempted to commit suicide at Weatherford, Texas, on the fifteenth instant. His life was saved.

A hotel at Conchis, Texas, was destroyed by fire on the sixteenth instant. A stranger from Arkansas called "Doctor," was burned to death.

Last week at Cedar Mills, Texas, the stores of Edlestines & Webb and Young & Raine, with contents, were destroyed by fire. The former was insured for $5000 and the latter for $5500.

Jim Morris who, with a man named Northcutt, murdered James Crabtree last fall, near Gordonsville, Texas, was captured in the Indian Nation last week, and was taken to Sherman for trial.

At Vaughan, Bosque county, Texas, last week, Warren Hill and Hugh Stull, prominent citizens, met and opened fire on each other. Three balls took effect upon Stull, killing him instantly.

At Socorro, Texas, Oriofrio Bacca, who murdered A. M. Conkling, editor of the Socorro Sun, was charged of by vigilant a few days since and strung up to the crossbeams of the gate in the courthouse yard.

At El Paso, Texas, last week, H. B. True, hailing from Los Angelos, California, was arrested and imprisoned on the charge of stealing a watch from Dr. J. F. Matchet, of Brenham, Texas, while he was dozing at the hotel.

At Matagorda, Texas, last week, Deputy Sheriff Ham Rigley was accidentally killed by a young lady, who, pointing a pistol at him, playfully said, "I believe I will shoot you, Ham." She fired, and Rigeley fell dead at her feet.

George T. Chamberlain, alias Yorke, who murdered a man in McCulloch county, Texas, in 1879, and for whose arrest a reward of $1600 was offered, was a few days since captured in the Indian Nation and taken to Fort Worth for safe keeping.

At Mount Vernon, Arkansas, two men—Baker and Massey—engaged in a fight, and Mayor Holt attempted to separate them. Baker struck the mayor with a stick, knocking him down, when young Holt sailed in, and dangerously stabbed Baker with a pocketknife several times.

An El Paso, Texas, paper says six physicians have already camped there, in the healthiest city on the planet. A State National bank is to be opened there next week, new stores are opening and the demi monde and dancehouse girls are fast arriving there in guady squads, and have already become too bold.

Last week Henry Witchery, colored, was drowned in Chickamauga creek while ferrying over some horses with a canoe. A half-witted negro sat on the bank, saw him drown, and some time afterward quietly remarked to several white persons that his "pard" was under the water. Search was made and the body found.

Near Gainesville, Texas, last week, at a house of ill fame, Charley Murphy, Tom—— and Jack Cook engaged in a row, during which Cook left, but was at once fired upon by Murphy, the shot striking him in the arm. Murphy and Tom—— then rushed upon Cook, disarmed him, and while Tom—— held him Murphy placed a pistol at his breast and fired, killing him instantly. The murderers fled and escaped.

Last Saturday at Osceola, Arkansas, at the store of Brickey Bros., Messrs. Ed H. Mathes, James Leston, Hugh R. McVeigh, G. R. Brickey and Edward Parry, were discussing certain charges supposed to have been made by J. O. Blackwood against Mr. Mathes. The latter read to Mr. McVeigh his published card with reference to the statements and then said to McVeigh: "Sir you are the law partner and friend of John O. Blackwood, and I now give you notice that I intend to kill him on sight unless he retracts these charges." McVeigh gave information to Blackwood who prepared to arm himself, but in the meantime Mr. Mathes was arrested and put under bond to keep the peace for twelve months.

A Georgia Tragedy.
ATLANTA, GA., Sept. 13.—S. M. Masters was killed yesterday at 70-mile post while walking on the Air-Line railroad track in a state of intoxication. A white woman was outraged by a negro yesterday near Orchard Hill, Ga. The negro has since been arrested and identified by the woman.
orchard-hill-orchard-hill-1881-09.A2:
Praying for the President. STAMFORD, CONN., Sept. 13.—An immense union Garfield prayer-meeting was held in the Baptist church this morning, in accordance with the Governor's recommendation. A large collection was taken for the benefit of the Michigan sufferers. NEW HAVEN, CONN., Sept. 13.—Business here was suspended to-day, in accordance with Governor Bigelow's proclamation, in the stores and factories and the banks and public offices between ten a. m. and three p. m. Prayers were offered in churches of every denomination for the recovery of the President. The Congregational churches on the green united at the First Church. There is a hush on the streets and a general suspension of ordinary traffic. What Dr. Agnew Says.
PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 13.—Dr. Agnew in an interview to-night said that he did not regard the President's case as by any means a hopeless one, and added that he thought the President would receive much benefit from the pleasant weather which may reasonably be expected at Long Branch during this month and the next. Dr. Agnew stated emphatically that the President never had an abscess on the lung. It was merely a circumscribed inflammatory trouble in the nature of bronchial pneumonia.

The Followers of Wesley.

LONDON, Sept. 13.—The Methodist Ecumenical Conference to-day expressed strong feeling against the Methodists sending their children to Romish schools. On the subject of "Skepticism," Mr. Todd, of Philadelphia, said that skeptical science was a great enemy of the church.

The conference strongly condemned the theatres and dancing, Messrs. Diffen and Buckley, Americans, speaking in support of these opinions. Mr. Peck advocated religious entertainments as a counter attraction. A motion condemning the opium trade was introduced, but was referred to the business committee at the suggestion of Mr. Peck, because it contained words censuring the British government. A motion recommending legislation against the sale of liquor on Sunday will be submitted.

The Second Maine District.

LEWISTON, ME., Sept. 13.—Returns from most of the Second Congressional District, increase the majority of ex-Governor Dingley (Republican). So far Dingley has 10,096; Gilbert, 4,947; scattering, 232. Dingley's majority, 4,917. These towns gave 1,387 Republican majority last year. The towns to hear from gave 67 Republican majority last year. It is probable that Mr. Dingley's majority is about 5,000. Androscoggin complete give Dingley 2,153 majority; Oxford nearly complete, 1,100; Franklin, 700, and Sagadahoc, 1,050. The Republican vote is larger than usual on an off year.

Louisiana Lottery Prizes.

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 13.—The principal prizes in the Louisiana State Lottery, drawn today, are as follows: No. 47,313 drew $30,000, sold in New York; No. 83,657 drew $10,000, sold in Vincennes, Ind.; No. 3,742 drew $5,000, sold in New York; No. 32,618 drew $2,500, sold in Cultman, Ala.; No. 56,771 drew $2,500, sold in New York and Warsaw, Ind. The following drew $1,000 each: Nos. 10,922, New Orleans; 23,045, New York; 56,682, New York; 88,362, New York; 96,326, Chicago.

S. M. Masters was killed last Monday while walking on the Air Line Railroad track in a state of intoxication.

A meeting of citizens was held Monday at the Memphis Cotton Exchange for the relief of the Michigan sufferers.

A white woman was outraged by a negro Monday, near Orchard Hill, Ga. The negro has since been arrested and identified by the woman.
