Michael Reilly was killed and another man had his eyes nearly destroyed by the premature explosion of a blast in the Forest and Dean mine, near Newburg, N. Y.

It is expected that the star route cases will come before the grand jury of the Criminal Court at Washington this month, after the local cases have been disposed of.

European immigration is again on the increase. The Elbe brought 1,100 Germans and French, and the Stella 689. The steamers due this week, it is said, will come pretty full.

Fresh shocks of earthquake have occurred at various parts of the Neapolitan provinces. Few persons have been killed, but many were injured, and serious damage has been done to property.

Helena F. Ayers, eight years of age, rescued a younger child from the wheels of an ice cart, in Providence, and in doing so lost her own life. She fell under the wheels and her head was crushed.

Charles S. Wolfe, member of the Legislature from Union county, in a "card to the public," dated Lewisburg, Penn., September 9th, announces himself as an Independent candidate for State Treasurer.

The commission appointed by the Secretary of the Treasury to investigate charges against H. L. Dodge, Superintendent of the Mint at San Francisco, have concluded their labors, and submitted to the Secretary a report fully exhonoring Mr. Dodge.

Thomas Wheeler, a laborer, discharged by Mrs. Frank Cate, at Kittery, New Hampshire, attempted to kill her, on Friday, but missed. In running away from him she fell and broke one of her legs in two places. After the attempt Wheeler shot himself in
shire, attempted to kill her, on Friday, but missed. In running away from him she fell and broke one of her legs in two places. After the attempt, Wheeler shot himself in the breast, but may recover.

Governor Wiltz, of Louisiana, has issued a proclamation calling the Sheriffs, Assessors and Tax Collectors of the State to a conference at the State House in New Orleans, on October 19th, for the consideration of the grave defects in the laws regulating assessments and collection of taxes and licenses.

The Dublin correspondent of the Times says: "At a meeting at Kiltullah, Galway, Mr. Larkin, of the New York Irish World, made a violent speech, in which he declared that Irishmen should not pay rent except at the point of the bayonet or the mouth of the cannon. The land act, he said, was a fraud."

About seventy-five tramps recently boarded a freight train on the Pennsylvania Railroad near Middletown, Pa., and threatened the crew with violence if they were not allowed to ride. A special train with a posse of officers was sent from Middletown, and twenty one of the ruffians arrested. They are supposed to be part of a gang which has been depredating in Lancaster county.

Some additional facts have transpired concerning the suspension of the New York Silk Manufacturing Company of a character to excite remark. It is said that the company has sunk between $360,000 and $400,-000 since it was started eight years ago. Of the capital, the report is that nearly $300,000 was paid in, and that this has all been absorbed, leaving a deficiency of at least $75,-000 between actual assets and liabilities. The company is supposed to have some $50,000 paper afloat, which is about maturing.

A scheme for swindling the government has just been brought to light in New York. Two men, W. and J. Taylor, imported on the steamer Wisconsin two iron cylinders six feet long and eight inches in diameter, saying they were a new patent hat roller to be established in this country. Suspicion was excited, and the rollers were sent to the seizure room. There, on examination, they were found to be hollow, and filled with dies for making nuts, etc. The cylinders were appraised at £10 7s. with duty of 35 per cent., while the contents are valued at from £200 to £500 with a duty of 45 per

THE NEWS.
Abram Altman, who recently resigned the presidency of the Third National Bank of Buffalo, N. Y., has been arrested at the suit of the bank for a deficiency of $45,000. Altman has lost money by speculation. He was at one time worth half a million, and built a house costing $120,000, which he placed in his wife's name.

Eight of the robbers who, recently, robbed the train near Independence, Kansas, have been arrested. One of the robbers, a boy of 16 years, getting the information and names of the parties.

Governor Fremont, of Arizona, was in Washington in conference with the War Department, and it was decided to furnish the people of that Territory with arms to defend themselves against the Apache Indians.

The Wilmington, N. C., papers continue their reports of damage to property by the hurricane. The damage to property is estimated at $100,000.

The removal of Sitting Bull and his band of Indians from the Standing Rock agency has been safely accomplished. Sitting Bull had been very defiant and said he would die rather than go to Fort Randall, but careful preparations were made by the commanding officer. The band was surrounded by a square of soldiers and forced step by step down the bank and into the boat, which then started down the river to Fort Randall.. A nephew of Sitting Bull made some resistance and was knocked down by the butt end of a musket. A squaw of the band, rendered desperate by the removal, killed her child and tried to commit suicide.

Captain Henry W. Howgate did not appear in the Criminal Court, as had been publicly announced that he would; neither has he arrived in the city.

The Postmaster General has ordered the discontinuance of steamboat mail service on the route from New Orleans to Shreveport, La., a distance of 660 miles.

Special dispatches from Franklin, Mich., a little port on Lake Michigan, thirty-five miles above Traverse City, announce the wreck of the steamer Columbia, of the Northeastern line, involving a loss of fifteen lives.

Cornelius O'Leary and his wife and three children were poisoned by eating canned mackerel in Cincinnati. The symptoms indicated lead poisoning. At last accounts the sufferers were in a critical condition.

In the special election held for a representatised in Congress, to fill the vacancy cauaine, by the resignation of Mr. Frye, Maine, ex-Governor Dingley was elected.

The farmers of New Castle County, Delaware, propose to give a carload of wheat to the sufferers by the Michigan fire. The Pennsylvania Railroad will transport the car free over its lines.

General Hazen has received official advices of the safe arrival of the signal service expedition, under Lieutenant Greely, at Lady Franklin Bay, one month from leaving St. John's. All are well.

Mr. John King, Jr., has withdrawn his resignation as receiver of the Ohio and Mississippi Railroad, and asks that a thorough examination be made into his administration.

A call is issued for a national convention of representatives of the agricultural, manufacturing and commercial interests of the country, to be held in the Cooper Institute, New York city,

The new Claremont stock yards are now completed, and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad Company will hereafter deliver all stock arriving at Baltimore by that road at the new yards.

The entire business portion of the town of Beaver, Utah, with the exception of the court-house and a co-operative store, was burned.

A white woman was outraged by a negro near Orchard Hill, Ga. The negro has been arrested and identified.

Samuel Romey, the murderer of John Smith, was taken from jail at Owingsville, Ky., by masked men, and hanged.

General Ambrose Burnside, United States Senator, of Rhode Island, died at his home in that state, September 13, from heart disease.

PERSONAL.
Rev. Robert Matlock, a preacher reported to have been lynched by a mob in the Boston mountains, in Arkansas, some six months ago, it seems was not lynched, as he was recently seen near Corsicana, in this state. Matlock was the starter of a new religion, a sort of mixture of all creeds, and soon had a crazy following about him. In his fanaticism he denounced all who would not think as he did, and was particularly severe on a family named Miller. Finally one of the family, a young man about 20 years old, told him he must stop his abuse of his family or take the consequences. Thus ill feelings arose between them, which culminated in their meeting one day at a public gathering where they talked the matter over and agreed to forgive and forget their differences and shook hands on it. As young Miller turned away, after they had taken awhile, Matlock suddenly drew a long knife and cut Miller's throat, severing his head nearly from his body. The excitement was tremendous, and an indignant crowd went in pursuit of the fleeing Matlock, and, as he was not seen afterwards, it was concluded he was caught and hung.

Governor Crittenden, of Missouri, has offered a reward of $100 for the arrest of Louis Merrick, charged with the murder of James Maupin in Chariton county, that state. The governor is great on offering rewards and refusing requisitions.

Rev. Dr. George B. Russell has accepted the presidency of Palatine college, at Myerstown, Pennsylvania. He was formerly pastor of Washington mission, of the Reformed church in the United States.

Mr. Boehwer, aged 83 years, and for thirty years a prominent citizen of Brookville, Indiana, while hunting eggs in his hay loft, a few days ago, fell through a hatchway, and was instantly killed.

Ira Harris, not unknown in Dallas as receiver of the Dallas & Wichita railroad at one time, is one of the corporators of the new enterprise, "the Thor Ironworks," just starting in Kansas City.

Mr. James Gordon Bennett, of the New York Herald, has taken a party of friends to the Yorktown centennial in his own yacht, and they will live on board of her while there.

Judge Scofield, of the United States court of claims, has returned to Washington city after a considerable absence, recuperating his health during the summer months.

Ex-Senator Spencer, from Alabama, under the carpet-bag regime, is now in Washington city, and it is said he will be given a good position under the new government.

Miss Ida McCreary, first lady assistant in the public schools of Carbondale, Illinois, died, a few days ago, her death creating the profoundest sorrow among all classes.

G. E. Whitney, a prominent contractor on the Fort Wayne railroad, was run over by a freight car and killed at Hamlet station on that road a few days ago.

The senator for Ain, France, Monsieur Bonnet, in jumping a ditch recently, fell and broke both his legs. He was out gunning at the time.

Ex-Governor Routt, of Colorado, it is said, has been recommended by General Grant for postmaster-general when Mr. James retires.

Mr. and Mrs. Ferdinand Jones, of Chicago, who have spent some years in Europe, will spend the winter in Washington city.

The wife and children of Assistant Secretary of State Hitt are visiting the mother of Mrs. Hitt, at LaFayette, Indiana.

Henry Garfield, son of the late president, has been elected vice president of the freshman class at Williams college.

The mother of United States Senator Sewell is dangerously ill at her home in New Jersey.

Hon. A. G. Thurman, ex-United States senator from Ohio, has arrived home from Europe.

The life of General Burnside is to be written by Ben Perly Poore.

The mutual duties of the church deacon and the monkey are to gather in contributions while the organs plays.

A colored man of Lancaster, Pa., has been accused of stealing a church. When a darkkey once gets religion he wants all of it there is in the market.

The aut musical members of Cook's Presbyterian church, Toronto, succeed d a few days ago in driving the musically-inclined members from the sacred precincts of the church at the toes of their boots. The organ followed the retreating party.

It seems that Mr. Harrison is not the only "Boy preacher." One Meredith who is given the same title, has been on trial at Canton, Ill., before the Methodist conference, on charges of "swearing, drunkenness, lying, smoking and claiming t be a republican when he was a democrat."

At the recent Methodist conference at Cincinnati Bishop Wiley told the clergymen that they must not kiss women as it was a dangerous practice. Well, the churches will keep on until there won't be any fun left. The Presbyterians won't let people dance, the Methodists kick on smoking and kissing, and all the churches prevent something. It will get so after a while that all we can do will be to join the Baptists, and go in swimming. The Baptists will never go back on a fellow's going in swimming.

A great many preachers are unconsciously being converted to Ingersollism. At a

recent prayer meeting Beecher said he "did not give some of the patriarchs a very good character, either, nor find much to say in commendation of Joshua, while he asserted that, in his opinion, Jacob's twelve sons were little better than cut-throats. He added that the idea that God had the sulks, and was revengeful, was abhorrent to every broad soul. And yet Beecher cannot fill a house the way Inger-oll can, at a dollar a head. There is getting to be a good deal of this kind of task, and it annoys us old Presbyterians a good deal.

A Baptist preacher, John R. Yeatts, discovered the "Millennium Spring" on Greasey Creer, Ark. It flows from a mountain 400 feet high, is the color of cider, and tastes like apple brandy. An eye-witness says: "Those under the influence of the water are perfectly ecstatic, hugging and loving everything they meet. Old men and old women, young men and young ladies, embrace each other by hugging and kissing. I met an old white-haired man and woman—I suppose about eighty years old—and they were hopping and skipping like lambs. I saw hundreds lying around the spring so drunk that they could not stand up, and they were lying and laughing trying to clap their hands."

Iev. Robert Matlock, some two years ago a Methodist minister in Arkansas, found the creed of that church too narrow for a man of such broad gauge as he was, and he jumped the game and established a religion of his own. The chief feature of Matlock's religion was blood atonement, and he used to slaughter lambs and burn them on an altar. Of course he got quite a following, as there is always an element in every community ready to embrace anything new in religion or politics. Another feature of Matlock's religion was the plain manner of which he called sinners liars and thieves. He would point out persons in the congregation, denounce them as sinners, and show that a sinner was either a liar or a thief. Of course the parties felt they were sinners, great sinners, and were willing to admit it, but they did not think it necessary to speak of it in such plain terms and in so personal a manner. On one occasion Matlock assailed a sinner named Tom Miller, gently chiding him for being a liar and a thief, and said it would be necessary for him to make a blood atonement. Miller got on his ear, and after church was over wanted to know what Matlock meant. Matlock then stabbed Miller to the heart, as a blood atonement, and was sent to an insane asylum for a year. The other day he was released, and a party of Miller's friends got hold of him and hung him up to a tree. They did not state what their reasons were, but the inference is that it was for a blood atonement.

Arrival of President Whitney

Special Telegram to the Examiner.

HOUSTON, November 28.—C. A. Whitney, president of the Central road, and George Schreiver, a big railroad man of New York, are in the city. This visit is taken as a confirmation of the rumor that Huntington is soon to get the Central, although Central officials deny the truth of such report.

FROM CORSICANA.

Escaped Ten Shots--All the Lawyers Indicted.

Special Telegram to the Examiner.

CORSICANA, November 28.—Deputy Sheriff Tom Trammell arrested a man named Williams in this county for horse stealing. When about six miles from here Williams put spurs to his horse and escaped, though shot at ten times by Trammell.

Nearly all the lawyers of Corsicana have been indicted by the grand jury, and will be tried to-morrow for nonpayment of the occupation tax.

Deputy Sheriff J. W. Evans, with Capt. James Garifty in charge as a witness in the Hurlock land fraud case, leave for Austin to-night.

Gratifying Intelligence.

It will indeed be gratifying intelligence to his many friends and to all property-holders of the city to know that Mr. J. A. Solomon, present alderman from the Third ward, has, after repeated and urgent solicitation on the part of his constituency, reluctantly consented to allow his name to go before the voters for re-election. pecuniarly Mr. Solomon is as largely interested as perhaps any other citizen of the city, and this is a guarantee that his official conduct will be in accord with the true interests of the city. He is also pre-eminently clear-headed, practical and energetic, and his past record stands as clean as that of any other alderman. Always prudent, Mr. Solomon is yet always aligned with the element which moves forward in the direction of making Waco a representative city, content to utilize to the fullest extent the means in hand, but seeking some means of replacing and enlarging these means to secure the maximum of result with the minimum of expenditure. The city is heartily glad the gentleman has allowed the use of his name.

Close of a Well-Spent Life.

On Sunday there died in West Waco, of pneumonia, after a week's illness, a man who is extensively known and respected, Mr. John. Cahill, aged 57 years. Deceased was born and reared in county Limerick, Ireland, but has been a citizen in the United States for some years. At the time of his death Mr. Cahill was foreman for J. D. Lynch, a Narrow Gauge contractor, but has been known as a contractor for some years, having spent some time on Iowa roads. He has been a resident of Texas since 1873, and leaves a wife and daughter at Whitehouse, a point on the International railroad in Smith county. The family will arrive on the Narrow Gauge this morning. The funeral services will take place at the Catholic church this morning at 10 o'clock, from whence the remains will be taken to the Catholic cemetery for interment. In learning of the death of Mr. Cahill railroad men in different sections of the country will regret to know of the close of a life that had in it much more of goodness and the elements of a true friend than aught else.

SERIOUS AFFRAY ON THE ISLAND. Desperate Encounter Between a Mob of Roughs and Two Police Officers.
One of the usual Sunday afternoon brawls on the Island happened yesterday afternoon. Ellen Duckett, a notorious colored "vag" and smasher generally, was drunk and creating a disturbance on Third and L streets southwest, and Officers Branson and Howell, of the First Precinct Station, attempted to arrest her. Immediately an immense mob led by her brother, Sam Duckett, a notorious thief and rowdy, surrounded the officers and tried to rescue the prisoner. A terrible fight ensued, in which Bransom was struck several times with stones and thrown down and his clothes nearly torn from his body, his club, badge, and belt, being wrenched away. Meanwhile Howell was wrestling with the Duckett woman, and, as she is as strong as any man, he had a hard time of it. During the scrimmage she bit his first finger nearly off, bit through the palm of his right hand, and laid his head open with a stone. Branson managed to release himself, and, drawing his pistol, fired, and saw a man drop to the ground face downwards. Branson rushed forward to secure his man, but was called by Howell to come to his rescue, and help take Ellen to the station-house, which they at last succeeded in doing. Returning to the scene of action they found that the man hit was Sam Duckett, and made vigilant search to find him, but he had been spirited away and it was impossible to discover his whereabouts. The officers continued searching until a late hour, but have not succeeded in finding him, he evidently having been secreted in some low shanty. From the way Duckett fell, the color of the blood, and the size of the pool it is presumed he was hit in the right side, near the region of the heart. Whether the wound is mortal remains to be seen. This Duckett woman has just returned from serving a six months' sentence in jail for biting Officer Branson's shoulder. Twelve of the participants in the fray have already been arrested and lodged in the station-house.

A very enjoyable Christmas entertainment occurred on Saturday evening at the New York Avenue Church. Practical charity was blended with the pleasure which the scholars of the Sunday school enjoyed, and in the room up-stairs contributions of groceries, money, clothing, &c., were liberally made for the poor of the Bethany and Gurley Missions. The children collected in the room down-stairs, and in one corner a series of beautiful tableaux held their attention and elicited numerous expressions of delight from the little ones. One tableau was entitled "The Choice," and another represented in a very effective way "The Closing and the Coming Year." These were interspersed with exercises appropriate to the occasion, under the direction of the superintendent, Mr. Williams. The church precentor, Mr. Kohr, rendered in his usual acceptable manner two solos, entitled "The Tar's Farewell" and "The Tin Soldier." Mr. Smith, the popular Sabbath school precentor, led the school in singing a number of Christmas carols. At the conclusion of the exercises he was presented by the teachers with a handsome easy chair. The entertainment closed in a manner that was highly satisfactory to the children by the distribution of candies and other Christmas presents.

Two Policemen Attacked by a Mob. ONE OF THE OFFICERS SHOOTS A MAN.
The denizens of a neighborhood in South Washington called "Fredericksburg" made a serious assault on Policemen Branson and Howell, of the South Washington precinct, about 3 o'clock Sunday afternoon. Officer Howell attempted to arrest a notorious colored woman named Ellen Duckett, at the corner of 3d and M streets southwest, for being disorderly and blowing a tin horn on the street. She fought like a wildcat, and bit the officer's arms and hands. Within a few minutes there were at least fifteen hundred people on the spot, most of them colored. A large crowd of colored men and women attacked the officers with sticks and stones, and the fight lasted half an hour. Sam Duckett, Ellen's brother, who is a desperate character, was one of the foremost of the crowd of roughs that assaulted the officers. He had a large stone in his hand, with which he struck Officer Branson in the breast, and was in the act of picking up another stone when the policeman fired and Duckett fell. The officer, thinking he had killed his assailant, went to the assistance of his partner, who was hard pressed by the crowd and bleeding from bad cuts on the head and bites on the hands and arms. The woman was finally gotten to the station house and locked up. After relieving his partner Branson went to look for the man he had shot, but could find nothing but a pool of blood. The officers have received information that the bullet struck Duckett on the back of the head and glanced around between the scalp and the skull and came out at his forehead. In the Police Court yesterday Ellen Duckett was charged with assaulting Officer Howell. There being some doubt as to whether this court can send a prisoner to jail for a year, the court sentenced her to eleven months and twenty-nine days in jail. Sam Berry, one of the crowd, was charged with disorderly conduct, and fined $10 or 30 days in the workhouse. Agnes Ware, alias Lucas, was also arrested for being disorderly in the crowd, and was fined $5 or 15 days.

Christmas Boat Racing on the Potomac.

The Potomac Boat Club yesterday afternoon gave two races on the river. The first race, for single sculls, was called at one o'clock. The course was from the "Three Sisters," a mile down the river. W. F. Roberts, W. C. Bailey and A. W. Harrison, were the starters. Roberts took the lead. When the bridge was reached all three were well together. Harrison spurted and took the lead. Roberts tried to capture it from him but could not. Harrison came in first, Roberts second, and Bailey last. Time, 6 minutes, 30 seconds.

The second race was for four-oared shells. It was from opposite the Potomac boat-house to the Aqueduct and return. The light-weight crew consisted of Harrison, bow; Roberts, 2; Whittington, 3, and Barbarin stroke; colors, white. The heavy crew was Bailey, bow; Johnson, 2; Zappone, 3, and Doyle stroke; colors, red. There was a good race to the turn. The light-weightts started back with a lead of two lengths. The race was hotly contested. The light-weightts, however, went ahead with a spurt and crossed the line about a length ahead of the heavies. The time was 7 minutes and 4 seconds.

DEATH OF AN OLD CITIZEN.—Mr. Amon Duvall, a well-known citizen of the District, father of Police Officer Edward Duvall, died on Saturday at his home, No. 216 G street, in the 68th year of his age. Mr. Duvall was a native of Baltimore, but resided in this city nearly all his life. In ante bellum days he was a member of the old police force—the Auxiliary Guard—and for a number of years was one of the guards of the jail. He was one of the earliest republicans in the District, and took part in the organization of the Wide Awakes years ago. He was a member of the Grand and Metropolis Lodge of Odd Fellows, who this afternoon attended his funeral.

Sam Duckett's Condition.
The negro, Sam Duckett, who was shot in South Washington Sunday night by Officer Branson, has been located, and will, if he is in a fit condition, be brought at once to justice. It is said that the ball entered the back of the man's head and passed out through the forehead, inflicting a painful but not necessarily dangerous wound. Duckett is a well known bruiser, and has, in the past, given the police a great deal of trouble. He is a vicious rascal, and if he were to die from his wounds, the community would not be very much distressed.

GUITEAU TRIAL CONTINUED.
DR. GRAY CROSS-EXAMINED.
HE THINKS THE PRISONER FEIGNING.
The witness having referred to the change in views among scientific men regarding insanity, the prisoner said: "Which shows that these experts don't know anything about it. They will swear to things to-day that they wouldn't have thought of swearing to 20 years ago and wouldn't swear to 20 years hence. The science of insanity is a progressive one."

Later the prisoner announced: "The idea that a man can't be insane without disease of the brain is nonsense. Read what the Saviour says. It is spiritology, not craniology, we want in this case."

The witness having said he was influenced in coming here by the advice of the president of the board of managers of the asylum, as well as the summons of the government, the prisoner asked: "How about Corkhill's money?"

Turning to the district attorney, the prisoner said: "He's got a bung hole up there at the Treasury which he had better shut off. He has run out $100,000 on this case I understand. He'll get shut off himself, I guess, before he's many days older. If I was President, he wouldn't be here a week. I will attend to him in '84 if Arthur doesn't attend to it before."

RECESS.

The court then, at 12:30, took a recess for half an hour.

GUITEAU ON THE AUTOGRAPH BUSINESS.

When the court reassembled Guiteau was the first to break silence. He said: "As there is nothing else to do, I might as will write my autographs for any one who wants them without money and without price. I wouldn't take—if I could get $500 for my autograph I wouldn't touch it. There's no money in this business for me. I don't care that there should be; I don't want any money about it—not one cent."

THE CROSS-EXAMINATION OF DR. GRAY

was then resumed by Mr. Scoville.

The witness said he had never had a case of insanity that he didn't find some disease of the body reflected in the brain, or some actual disease of the brain itself.

Mr. Scoville having asked if he had examined the brains of all his patients, the witness said:—
“We don't kill a man in order to examine his brain.”
“I didn't know what modern science might do,” remarked Mr. Scoville.

GUITEAU ON KILLING A MAN TO EXAMINE HIS BRAIN.

“That's the way these fellows do,” said the prisoner. “They kill a man and then examine his brain. That's what the experts are trying to do on this case, I suppose.”

Mr. Scoville questioned the witness upon an article he published in 1874 in the American Journal of Insanity on the “Pathology of Insanity.”
“Write something, doctor, on spiritology of insanity, next time,” interjected the prisoner.

FEIGNED INSANITY.

The witness said he had investigated 40 or 50 cases of feigned insanity.

“Did you ever,” asked Mr. Scoville, “know of any case of feigned insanity like that of the prisoner?”

“I have not considered,” the witness replied, “that the prisoner at the bar has made any manifestation of insanity.”

The witness was asked if he had not testified that the prisoner was feigning, and he replied that he said he was feigning in so far as he tried to impress people that he was acting under an inspiration.

Mr. Scoville asked to have evidence on this point stricken out, as “now he has”—began Mr. Scoville, “Put his toot into it,” interjected the prisoner.

“Let the cat out of the bag,” continued Mr. Scoville.

The witness has now declared that his belief is “that the prisoner is telling a lie.”

The witness insisted that he based his judgment on the prisoner's conduct.

“It is a fact for the jury to pass upon,” said the prisoner, “whether he refers to the testimony or my conduct.”

The witness said he did not pass upon the question whether the prisoner was lying or not.

“I never lie, sir,” shouted the prisoner.

The court overruled Mr. Scoville's objection to the testimony.

“All your talk is different from what you said yesterday,” said the prisoner to the witness. “Corkhill must have demoralized you last night.”
"All your talk is different from what you said yesterday," said the prisoner to the witness. "Corkhill must have demoralized you last night? How much are you going to get for this extra work? It ought to be worth about a thousand dollars more than it was yesterday."

The witness, having declined to answer a question categorically, the prisoner remarked: "The doctor is getting badly demoralized this afternoon."

Mr. Scoville having questioned the witness in reference to the delusions of drunken men, the prisoner said: "According to your philosophy, doctor, a man can't get drunk or crazy without his brain is diseased. That shows how much you know about it."

The witness said insanity could not be produced by fear or other emotions without an intermediate physical disturbance. This disturbance might come from the quickened action of the heart, cau sing a fusion of blood in the brain.

GUITEAU'S NEW YEAR GREETING.

The cross-examination dragged along until nearly 3 o'clock, when the prisoner stopped it by saying: "It's most 3 o'clock, Scoville. To-morrow will be New Year's day, 1882. I receive my calls this year at the jail; any one who comes can get in. I will be glad to see any one who comes. I wish everybody a happy New Year's."

The court was then adjourned till Tuesday.

MRS. ELIZARETH A. BALL, wife of Mr. Robert Ball, (one of our well-known citizens,) and a lady beloved by all who knew her, died about noon today, aged 52 years, at her residence, 233 G street. The funeral will be Monday afternoon.

THERE WAS A STAMPEDE and almost a panic yesterday afternoon at the government printing office by the cracking of a timber or an iron bolt connected with the building, making a jarring of the whole structure and a report loud enough to be generally heard. As no evil results followed, the employees returned somewhat timidly to their work again. The occurrence has been kept quiet by the employees there. Mr. Entwisle, the building inspector, states that United States government buildings do not come under his jurisdiction, but under that of Mr. Edward Clark, at the Capitol, for examination as to safety.
LET HIM OFF EASY BECAUSE HE WAS SHOT IN THE HEAD.—Sam Duckett, the notorious negro rough, who assaulted Officer Branson while attempting to make an arrest in South Washington Christmas day, and who was shot in the head by the officer, was up for trial at the Police Court this afternoon, and through his attorney, Mr. H. H. Wells, Jr., he entered a plea of guilty. The court said that in consideration of the suffering he has undergone from the pistol-shot wound he would only impose a fine of $10 or thirty days.

SUIT AGAINST MRS. MYRA CLARK GAINES.—Mary Ellen Randolph to-day, by Messrs. Durant and Horner, filed a bill against Mrs. Myra Clark Gaines. Plaintiff is the widow and residuary legatee of W. M. Randolph, who died January 8th, 1876, who was employed in the prosecution of Mrs. Gaines' claim against the estate of Daniel Clark, for which she became indebted to him $10,000, payable at the rate of $2.50 on each $100. She therefore prays a decree for the same and for discovery of the amounts Mrs. Gaines has obtained judgments for.

“RED BILL” ARRESTED FOR THE ROBBERY AT THE CAPITOL.—Officer S. P. Hineline, of the 5th precinct, last night arrested a man who gives his name as Charles Howard, but who is known by the police as “Red Bill,” on suspicion of being the thief who stole the $285 yesterday morning from Mr. Winship, late paying teller under Sergeant-at-Arms Thompson, at the Capitol, as mentioned in THE STAR. The arrest was made at the instance of Detectives Miller and McElfresh, who were aware of “Red Bill's” arrival in this city. He is said to be a sneak thief, burglar, and “hoister,” and an expert in all. He hails from Boston, but has recently been operating in Baltimore as a “holiday hoister” or shop-litter; and has also had experience in bank work. He is 27 years old, and gives his occupation as machinist. He is at police headquarters.

Snow Blockade.

A Brutal Affair.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

New York, February 15—10 p. m.—A desperate fight took place on Long Island yesterday, for five hundred dollars a side, between two English bull terrier dogs, "Toboy" and "Paddy," twenty pounds weight each. The contest lasted a little over five hours, and both dogs were torn nearly to pieces. After the fight "Toby" fell into a fit and died. Before the fight was over outsiders interfered and caused the fight to be drawn.

False Reports.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

WASHINGTON, February 15—1 a. m.—Gen. McDowell telegraphs from San Francisco to the war department that advises from the Apache country and southeastern Arizona, prove that the recent sensational stories of Indian atrocities there are false.

Honors to Archbishop Feenan.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

Chicago, February 16—1 a. m.—A very fine reception was tendered Archbishop Feenan last night at the rooms of the Young Men's Catholic association. About 2,000 of the better class of Catholics attended, and were formally presented to the new prelate by Judge Moran.

Arrest of Two Young Sports.

Special Dispatch to The Bee

Chicago, February 16—1 a. m.—Two young men were yesterday observed by a policeman in a hack acting suspiciously. He followed them to a clothing store, where they made large purchases, displaying quantities of money. The officer arrested them, and took them to a station, where $5,500 were found in their possession.

One of them gave the name of John M. Dalton, from Milwaukee, and when closely questioned confessed he had found the money in that city Monday night, and came here to have a good time with his friend. It was learned that James S. White, ex-city comptroller of Milwaukee, had been about the saloons and restaurants of that city Monday night, freely displaying a large amount of money, said to have been $8,500 in cash and certificates. This he shortly afterwards missed, but could not tell whether he had lost it or it had been stolen from him. The police here think the money found on Dalton belongs to White, and have communicated with the Milwaukee police, holding Dalton in custody.

Snow Bound.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

St. Paul, February 16—1 a. m.—Reports are still coming in from the back country districts of the great snow storm of Friday. Some of the railroads are still seriously embarrassed, but trains on most of them manage to get through. Farmers and villagers are badly snowed up in many localities.

Des Moines, Iowa, February 16—1 a. m.—Trains on all the trunk lines got through yesterday, but the storm set in again last night and the Northwestern is blocked again. The Fort Dodge road is still blocked, and it will require several days to get through.

Ivory Punching.

Special dispatch to The Bee.

New York, February 16—1 a. m.—The billiard match last night between Jacob Schaefer and William Sexton, 400 points, cushion caroms, for a purse of $1,000, was won by the former in 110 lanterns. Schaefer, 400; Sexton, 396. The winner's average was 3 7 11. Time of game, 2 hours and 44 minutes.

Remnants of the Cave-Dwellers.

Special Dispatch to The Bee

SPRINGFIELD, Ky., February 16—1 a. m.—A few days since, while exploring Smoky Cave, on the farm of Mr. Hay, Dr. Briggs found six skeletons of human beings. He says they are those of an ignorant people, for they have low and receding foreheads. Remnants of rudely-made cooking utensils were also found in that vicinity. He thought the shape of their skulls were characteristic of the Indian, but the fact of cast iron vessels being found, was indicative of a higher class of people having resided there.

Captured His Man.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

MOBILE, Ala., February 16—1 a. m.—A report reaches here of a terrible tragedy which was enacted at Escatampa, Washington county, Ala., about eight o'clock last night. James Orzo, white, and Sampson Daker, colored, had a fight, and Hunter bruised Orzo with an axe handle. They were separated, and Orzo, being a justice of the peace, with three men afterward attempted to arrest Hunter, who resisted with an axe. He was shot in the breast by Orzo with a shot gun, and died in a few minutes.

Crushed and Baked.

Special Dispatch to the Bee

NEW YORK, February 16—1 a. m.—A Wilmington, N. C., special says: Five men were killed and two injured near Carthage Monday night. A windstorm blew two large trees upon a cabin occupied by the men in the turpentire works, and crushed five to death. The cabin then took fire and burned up with the five bodies in it.

Revenged at Last.

Special Dispatch to The Barr.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., February 16—1 a.m.—A special to The Commercial from Lawrenceburg, Ky., says a terrible tragedy was enacted in the county jail at that place yesterday afternoon. Thomas Agae, who was in jail for shooting Martin Sames a year ago, killed the latter, who had just been arrested for arson. The man's throat was cut, and he was stabbed in four places. The town people threaten to lynch the murderer. The coroner's jury returned a verdict of unjustifiable murder.

A treaty has been concluded between Barrie and Giles.
sampson-hunter-escatampa-1881-02-15.A2: Saturday, 12:b, at 9 o'clock p. m., a fearful tragedy was enacted at Escatawpa, Washington county, Ala. From Mr. W. T. Miller, who reduced to writing the evidence before the jury of inquiry, we obtain the following particulars: About S o'clock p. m. Jas. Orso, white, and Sampson Hunter, colored, got into a quarrel, ending in blows, Sampson striking Orso with an exe handle, it is supposed, as the handle was found there after the difficulty, and Orso was considerably bruised. They were then separated. Sampson lived in a shanty owned by E. Garrettson, and worked for Garrettson. After this difficulty Sampson went home. Orso, being a justice of the peace, determined to arrest Sampson for a breach of the peace, and at nine o'clock, accompanied by Cessford, Malono and O'Denell, went to his shanty for that purpose. Garrettson heard of it and wont down to quiet the matter, and received a lick upon the left side of his head above the eyebrow and ear, from whom it is not known, which knocked him senseless. Sampson refused to surrender and the party rushed in upon him. He was armed with a turpentine ax and offered resistance with it. Orso, having a double-barrel shotgun, fired upon Sampson, breaking his right arm and sending one ball into his right breast below the nipple and raging toward the bowels. Sampson continued a very vigorous resistance with the ax, and would have slain Orso had not Cessford knocked him down in time to prevent it. As he fell, Orso knocked at him with the butt end of his gun, but the gun hit a table and broke off the stock. He then turned the gun and struck again, breaking the barrels in two against the table. The parties then withdrew. Sampson lingered till 7 a. m. Sunday and died.

The Father of His Country. N. O. City Item.
N. O. City Item. The following beautiful epitaph was discovered on the back of a portrait of Washington, sent to the family from England. It was copied from a transcript in the hand-writing of Judge Washington : WASHINGTON :

The defender of his country—the founder of liberty—the friend of man. History and tradition are explored in vain for a parallel to his character. In the annals of modern greatness he stands alone; and the noblest names of antiquity lose their lustre in his presence. Born the benefactor of mankind, he united, all the qualities necessary to an illustrious career. Nature made him great; he made himself virtuous. Called by his country to the defense of her liberties, he triumphantly vindicated the rights of humanity, and on the pillars of National Independence laid the foundation of a great republic. Twice invested with supreme magistracy by the unanimous voice of a free people, he surpassed in the Cabinet the glories of the field, and voluntarily resigning the sceptre and the sword, retired to the shades of private life. A spectacle so new and so sublime was contemplated with the profoundest admiration, and the name of Washington, adding new lustre to humanity, resounded to the remotest regions of the earth. Magnanimous in youth, glorious through life, great in death; his highest ambition, the happiness of mankind; his noblest victory, the conquest of himself. Bequeathing to posterity the inheritance of his fame, and building his monument in the hearts of his countrymen, he lived the ornament of the eighteenth century, he died regretted by a mourning world."

A Desperate Fight In Washington County Alabama.

(Special to the Democrat)

MOBILE, Feb. 14.—A fearful tragedy has occured at Escatawba, Washington county, in this State. Jas. Orso justice of the peace, had a fight with Sampson Hunter, colored. At 8 o'clock that night Orso went with a posse and J. F. Garretson to arrest Sampson, who defended himself with a turpentine ax. In the row Orso fired on Sampson, breaking his arm and shooting him in the breast. Sampson would have overpowered Orso and killed him with the ax but was knocked off by one of the crowd and Orso beat his gun to pieces over him. Garretson received a blow on the head and is still insensible. Sampson has died. Orso is at home awaiting arrest.

LATE NEWS ITEMS.
The mining town of Alta, Utah, has been almost buried under the snow. A series of avalanches have occurred, causing the deaths of at least ten persons. The names given are Mrs. Haskins and her daughter Jane, Charles Borbridge, Frank Laporte, Robert Haworth, Van Morris, John Fitzgerald, P. B. Lee, Wm. Hollingshead, and a man named Darby. Richard Williams and John Washington are missing. Other disasters of a similar nature are reported from other localities in the Wahsatch and Big Cottonwood.

SECRETARY SHERMAN has been on a visit to Mentor.

The Greenback members of Congress sent a congratulatory telegram to Governor Plaisted, of Maine.

"Buck" Walsh, a noted burglar, sentenced to the Sing Sing (N. Y.) Prison for twenty years, was shot dead on the 15th by a guard while trying to escape.

Three men were recently lynched at Colorado, N. Mex., the present terminus of the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railroad, for having robbed a woman; and at San Marcial, a few miles distant, two desperadoes were disposed of in an equally summary manner by riddling their bodies with bullets.
At Point au Pelee Island, Lake Erie, on the 16th, a man named Reinheimer shot another, Andrew Henderson, a mail carrier, and then blew out his own brains. The two men had always been good friends, and insanity is suspected in the murderer, as he had previously attempted to take his own life.

Knox Pinckard and a colored servant were buried under a snowslide at Georgetown, Colo., both being dead when exhumed. William Pinckard escaped with his life.

The Texas & St. Louis Railroad has been compled to Corsicana, 203 miles from Texarkana.

It is reported from Tucson, Nev., that a stage from Messilla to Fort Cummings was attacked by Indians about ten miles Fort Cummings. The bodies of three men and one woman, passengers, were found mutilated and burnt. They were removed to Cummings. The Indians are supposed to have numbered forty. They were being pursued by troops.

Cal. Huey was hanged at Osceola, Ark., on the 14th, for the murder of John Broadway, in Crittenden County, in the fall of 1879.
THERE was no session of the Senate on the 15th. The debate on the Funding bill was further continued in the House, a large number of amendments being proposed and mostly rejected.

THREE MASKED MEN Make Quite a Hole in the Cash Balances of a Chicago Firm—Suspicion that the Janitor Knows More of the Affair Than will Prove Good for Him—A Suspected Murderer Caught in Canada-Registered Letter Robbery in Chicago-Not a Good Day for Voting, Either-An Army Paymaster Retired Other Crimes.
CLIFTON, January 24.—Dr. Thomas Aust, accused of murdering his brother-in-law, Jas. Humphrey, in Indiana, a short time ago, was arrested here Saturday.

Murdered and Burned.

ATLANTA, GA., January 22.—Carrie Stokes, colored, was murdered last night. Her body was placed on the fire, wood piled around it, and her clothing saturated with coal-oil. Her head and face were horribly burned.

Not Much of a Voter, After All.

CHARLESTON, January 24.—In the United States district court, Saturday, William L. Webb, white, of Georgetown county, was tried on the charge of voting twenty-one ballots at the last election. The jury returned a verdict of guilty, with a recommendation to mercy.

Bounced, Imprisoned and Fined.

WASHINGTON, January 24.—The President has approved the sentence of the general court-martial in the case of Paymaster J. H. Nelson, of the army, which is that he shall be dismissed from the service, confined two years at hard labor in the penitentiary (probably Albany) and fined $2500.

Robbery of Registered Letters.

Robbery of Registered Letters.

CHICAGO, January 24.—Four days ago the postoffice authorities here were surprised by finding a registered letter pouch from Rochester, New York, had been cut open and seventeen out of twenty-one valuable packages stolen. As five of the envelopes bore Robinson postoffice stamps, a telegram was sent there to ascertain their contents, and it was found that one contained ten dollars, three others five dollars each, and the fifth a ruby breastpin. From this Special Henshaw deduces that the total loss, which was at first rumored to be $150,000, does not exceed $200. The bag came over the Michigan Southern road, but whether the robbery took place on the train at the depot or in the Chicago postoffice is not known. The matter was kept a close secret by the postoffice authorities, in the hope of detecting the robbers.

Her Chances are Good.

HER CHANCES ARE GOOD.

LYNCHBURG, VA., January 24.—Suit has been brought in the United States district court in behalf of Millie T. Whitlow, a white girl living in Cumberland county. Miss Whitlow, it appears, has lived for some time in the family of a negro, as nurse and house servant, being treated and considered as one of the household, though nothing specific was alleged as to criminal conduct or character. This mode of life tended to injure her reputation in the neighborhood. After leaving the house of Coleman, the negro, the girl entered one of the public schools of the county as pupil, upon which the rest of the scholars all stopped attending it. The teacher applied for instructions to the school board, and was directed to exclude Miss Whitlow. He did so, and she now brings suit for damages, naming a round sum. All parties to the suit are white, but the girl lost her character by living with the negro as his servant. As this fact gives the Federal court jurisdiction it will be a point of no small importance. Alexander Rives, who recently caused the indictment of the State judges for failure to put negroes on their juries, will preside at the trial.

Brooks and the Burglar.

CHICAGO, January 24.—One of the boldest and most successful burglaries ever planned and executed in this city occurred about 7 o'clock last evening, at the office of the South Chicago Iron and Steel Works, on Ashland avenue, near Thirtieth street, but was not reported by the police until 2 o'clock this morning. It was then learned that three masked burglars had forced the office door, bound and gagged the janitor, Chas. Brooks, and while one of them stood guard over him with a pistol, the others drilled a hole in the safe, blew open the combination, and bidding the old watchman a cheerful good night, left, taking $1000 in five-dollar gold pieces, and $150 in coin, together with about $9000 in bills, done up in envelopes, ready for paying the help to-day. The above facts are given by Brooks, but the police regard something about the affair as sufficiently suspicious to implicate him, and have accordingly arrested him and his son. He told somewhat contradictory stories; his unruffled clothing and unprepossessing appearance raised doubts of his accuracy and integrity. Paddy Cavanaugh, a notorious character, was also arrested.

No Unnecessary Ceremony Over It.

Leadville, Herald: A former resident of

No Unnecessary Ceremony Over It.

Leadville Herald: A former resident of Leadville, who has just returned from Colorado, New Mexico, the present terminus of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railway, says a woman—Mary McBride—was making her way from Colorado, which is the terminus, to the old town, a distance of a mile and a half. She was walking along leisurely when she noticed four men coming toward her. They were very demonstrative, but she thought them endowed with sufficient humanity to respect a woman, and endeavored to proceed on her way. They surrounded and ordered her to give up her money if she had any. She declined to do so, when they adopted compulsory methods, and relieved her of $137, which was the last cent she had. The woman returned to the end of the track, and described the villains who had robbed her. That night three of the rufians were found playing cards in a saloon, and justice was indeed summary. Without a word the vigilantes walked forward, and seizing the highwaymen, and marched them out. Ropes were soon placed around their necks and they were dangling from the telegraph poles. The avengers returned to their homes as if nothing unusual had occurred. The next day the gentleman interviewed continued his journey, and arrived at San Marcial in good time to witness the invasion of the town by two desperadoes whose yells and carousals made the place hideous. Scarcely had he seated himself at the hotel table when shrieks and the firing of revolvers summoned the guests to their feet, and running out upon the piazza they could see the darkness broken here and there by the sharp flash of revolvers. In a moment the entire populace was up in arms and in pursuit of the disturbers, who ran their animals with break-neck speed to the old town of San Marcial. Here they repeated their deviltry, and entertained themselves by riding into a saloon, shooting out the lights, taking possession of the bar and running things generally. While they were in the saloon and had complete and undisputed possession of the place, citizens arrived from the new town, and approaching noiselessly, corraled the roughs. The proprietor had abandoned the place, and at the word the entire party opened fire on the usurpers. Volley upon volley was fired in upon them, and subsequent examination disclosed that seventy-one balls had found their way into the two bodies. The next day a hole was dug in the prairie and the dead men thrown into it.

NEWARK, December 13.—The agreement of the directors of the Mechanics' National Bank provides, it is understood, that the nine directors shall contribute $700,000 to pay depositors under $200 in full and the other depositors seventy-five per cent. within three months, provided the creditors agree to surrender their claims against the institution and relieve the stockholders of their assessment, provided the latter assign their shares to the person designated by the directors. The road is to be extended to Portsmouth, with a branch to Gallipolis. WHISPERINGS OF LOVE.—Your baby's life is in danger whenever it is troubled with a cough or cold. Give Dr. Bull's Cough Syrup. Price 25 cents. THETRIPLEMURDER At Aberdeen, Miss.—A Negro Accomplice Tells How the Foul Deed was Done—A Murderer Sulcides in Jail—Wife-Murder and Suicide—Sentenced to be Hanged—Found Guilty of Murder.
ABERDEEN, Miss., December 13.—The murderer of the Walker brothers is still at large. The negro under arrest has, after severe torture, told the story of the horrible scene. The negro was passing along the highway, and was attracted by a camp fire some distance from the road. One man was there awake by the fire, while the other three boys were asleep on a bed spread out before it. This man beckoned to the negro to come there, and disclosed to him his deadly purpose, saying to the negro that there was money in it, and promised to give him $200 for his aid in the execution of the blackest of deeds. The negro describes the procedure—the younger brother was asleep in the middle. The first killed was the youngest, who received two blows on the head with the ax; the next in age was the second victim. By this time the oldest brother had opened his eyes and raised his head, when the monster struck him one blow on the head that killed him instantly. They then covered the bodies with blankets, and after rifling their pockets of a watch and sixty dollars, the man handed the negro the ax, telling him to throw it out of sight, then mounted a mule, and has not been seen since.

Sentenced to be Hanged.

Sentenced to be Hanged.
St. Louis, December 13—Martin Packett, who shot and killed James Barnes in January, 1880, was found guilty of murder in the first degree, yesterday, at New Madrid, Missouri, and sentenced to be hanged on the 20th of January.

The Poughkeepsie Bank Defalcation.
Poughkeepsie December 13 The Daily

The Poughkeepsie Bank Defalcation.

POUGHKEepsie, December 13.—The Poughkeepsie bank defalcation of $50,000 is thought to be a deficiency in the county funds. Halloway, the cashier, is at his home in a state of extreme nervous prostration and is threatened with brain fever.

Found Guilty of Murder.

DETROIT, December 13.—Lambertus Vescamp was found guilty at Kalamazoo, this morning, of the murder of Lyman Cody, in Ottawa county, in May last. The trial lasted over a week. The defense set up insanity. The jury was out an hour and a half. The verdict gives great satisfaction, as the public are getting rather tired of the insanity plea in murder cases. Vescamp was sentenced to the State's prison for life, the extreme penalty in this State.

Wife-Murder and Suicide.

DETROIT, December 13.—A double tragedy occurred at Cold Water at an early hour this morning in a house of ill-fame kept by Mrs. Nettie Wheeler, better known as "Net Davis." While entertaining some company about 1 o'clock with vulgar songs, sung by herself and her girls, her husband called her into the kitchen and remonstrated against any further singing of the sort, when she replied, "I will not, if you wish it." He immediately shot her through the breast, when she ran to the parlor and fell dead. The murderer then put three bullets into his own body, which resulted fatally at once. Jealousy was the supposed cause.

Tired of Life.

Tired of Life.

CINCINNATI, December 13.—The Gazette's Dayton (O.) special says that Mason S. Hamilton shot himself to-day in the oathhouse of a saloon, and when found was insensible. The ball having entered his head near the left eye and passed out near the ear, the surgeon declared that death was inevitable. He left a letter to the Coroner, saying that he took his own life because of ill health and inability longer to enjoy life. He was Captain of Company H of the Eleventh Indiana Cavalry during the war; had been County Surveyor of Butler county and City Solicitor of Hamilton, Ohio. For the past two years he had been an inmate of the Soldiers' Home.

A Murderer Commits Suicide in Jail.

DETROIT December 13. L. W. Dixon the

DETROIT, December 13.—J. W. Dixon, the man arrested on the charge of having murdered Wm. J. Phillips, the drover, in Sanitac county, as telegraphed yesterday, died this morning in jail from the effects of laudanum taken early Monday morning. He was informed by his physician that he could not possibly live, and was asked if he had anything to say. He replied: "No; nothing. I want to die." He was delirious most of last night, but would divulge nothing, and would often repeat the words, "Poor Phillips! he is dead!" The prosecution had worked up a strong case against Dixon. Phillips was known to have been on the up train November 25th, and got off at Amadore. That same day Dixon hired a rig at Lexington, which he returned the following day. The night of the 25th he called at a farmhouse, near Amadore, and asked for a pair of hot water, saying his horse was foundered. The folks noticed blood on his hands, and a boy says he saw him washing the buggy. The buggy was examined yesterday, and clots of blood found in the crevices. Dixon had also displayed large amounts of money within the last two weeks, which was something very unusual with him. He also tried to purchase a brick block at Lexington, offering $3000 cash for it. Telegrams had passed between Phillips and Dixon, which the prosecution were unable to get at present, but it is thought they will be conclusive of his guilt. Dixon's relatives live at Mount Clemens, and he leaves a family. Some years since he was sent to the State prison for forgery.

There is an unusually large number of candidates for the various offices within the gift of the Legislature.

A. T. Roane, of Calhoun county, is an applicant for the position of circuit judge of the third district.

A great many colored people are leaving Noxubee county for Alabama and the bottom lands of this State.

Meridian has a beggar who refuses to take more than a nickle. If a half dollar is handed to him, he hands it back.

A club of Port Gibson men had 83 lottery tickets in the last drawing in the Louisiana lottery, and only drew $7.
Many of the persecuted Russian Jews are settling in different portions of the State. They are generally gladly welcomed.

Capt. A. B. Shropshire, of Columbus, who was sent to the penitentiary for stealing a steamboat, has been pardoned by the Governor.

Anderson Lewis, (c) of Lauderdale county, who was serving a sentence of 15 years in the penitentiary, has been pardoned by Gov. Stone.

One night last week the boys of Louisville built ten rail fences across some of the principal streets, and placed bales of cotton in the houses of many people.

One McDaniel, a colored man of Tishomingo county, stole some soda, as he thought, but after he had used it in buscuit, it turned out to be rat poison and killed him.

A rattlesnake measuring 15 inches in diameter and 11 1/2 feet in length, and having 19 rattles, was killed in Natchez last week. When shot the snake had a large rabbit in its mouth.
In Warren county, on the 22d inst., Merritt Henry, colored, was killed by Frank Lamar, an Italian, from whom he had stolen a pound of cheese. This caused the killing.

A few days since near Jaciato, Alcorn county, Jeff Boone, a colored mail carrier, was shot and killed as he neared a deep ravine, by somebody concealed in the woods—it is supposed. The motive of the murderer is not known.

William Miller, colored, and Robert Jones, murderers of the Walker brothers, are in jail at Aberdeen. They will be tried at a special term of court, to begin on January 30th. There can be little doubt about hanging them without delay.
At the recent meeting of the State Grange in Durant, 159 Granges represented 53 counties. A resolution favoring the repeal of the lien law was passed unanimously by a rising vote. This was the largest meeting of the State Grange since 1876.

Raid on Salloons. CINCINNATI, December 24.—A body of masked men, supposed to be the best citizens of the place, broke into all the drinking saloons in Cedarville, Greene county, Ohio, at 3 o'clock this morning, and wholly destroyed all the liquors on hand. Some of the buildings were almost torn down. Much excitement prevails. The loss is reported as reaching into thousands of dollars, but no definite estimate is made. Cedarville is a village of unusually good reputation for morality. Great Revival in Mexican Mining Interests. TUCSON, ARIZ, December 24.—Sheriff De Long has returned from a trip to Sonora, and reports a great revival in mining interests. Much American capital is flowing into the northern districts. Governor Ortiz is especially interested in encouraging the immigration of Americans.
New York politics seem to be in a muddled condition. The Democratic party is now divided into four organizations, each

claiming to be the simon-pure article, and neither being willing to strike their flag with the view of securing harmony and concert of action. According to the New York Times, things are not much better in the Republican party in that city. It says the twenty-six district associations are masters of the situation, and only their enrolled members, who number about 10,000, can take part in the primaries. The presidents of these associations are, or represent, the managers. Of the twenty-six presidents chosen last week sixteen are officeholders, drawing about $50,-000 a year, and two more are "dummies" for officeholders.

AT THE SCENE OF HIS CRIME.

Detective Bean Arrives at Aberdeen With Bob Jones, the Murderer of the Walker Brothers.

The Villain Makes a Full Confession of the Terrible Crime, in All its Hideous Details.

Special to the Appeal.]

ABERDEEN, Miss., December 24.—Mr. Rush O. Bean, the detective who left here some days ago in search of Bob Jones, the murderer of the three Walker boys killed near here about one month ago, arrived in Aberdeen last night with the prisoner. For the capture of this villain Mr. Bean deserves not only the rewards he received, but the thanks of all interested in peace and the sanctity of society. The miserable wretch evaded, lied and dissembled to such an extent that eavesdropping was found necessary, and this being done the listener succeeded in hearing the plot of the murder, the deed and all subsequent transactions, as William Miller, the negro accomplice, was incarcerated with Jones in the same cage; however, to make sure of the identity and guilt, to-night the negro was taken from jail under the threat and pretext of being lynched. This left Jones alone in his dreary dungeon, in darkness and horror. Two gentlemen then approached Jones, and, after diligent effort, succeeded in procuring a full confession to the heinous crime. He confessed having split the heads of the three boys as they lay by the fireside of their camp beside the road, having taken their money, and his escape and subsequent flight and capture. This murder being the most horrible ever known in this community, great interest was felt, and his capture is a relief to this entire section. He will be tried with Miller at a special term of the court, and they will speedily be sent to the happy hunting grounds.

GOVERNOR CHURCHILL Taking Things Quietly, and Expects to be Able to Show an Error in the Committee's Report. A Theatrical Man Leaves Little Rock on Short Notice—Business Assignment—Mill Destroyed.
Special to the Appeal.

LITTLE ROCK, December 27.—Governor Churchill and attorney have been to-day arranging a programme for the rebuttal of the alleged facts presented by the Senate investigating committee, showing a defalcation when he was Treasurer. The merchants and others who are on his bond show a more quiet spirit to-day, alleging that he can show an error in the committee's report.

ASSIGNMENT.

J. & L. Ehrenberg, wholesale liquor merchants, who made an assignment to-day, made their brother, H. Ehrenberg, a preferred creditor for $3000.

COULDN'T FACE THE MUSIC.

Stanley, business manager of Rice's Evangeline troupe, took a fly-by-night trip to Mabelville last night to avoid meeting Mr. Deshon, proprietor of the Capital Hotel, who desired to interview him concerning the authorship of an article reflecting on Deshon published in a Louisville paper. Stanley's trip was made in a buggy, which upset, injuring him, not seriously. This troupe closes its engagement here to-night.

Mill Blown Up with Fatal Results.

[Associated Press Report.]

LITTLE Rock, December 27.—The Gazette's Gurdon special says that Wilson's mill, at that place, was blown up last evening, killing Charles Heel, fatally wounding Cool French, and seriously injuring Allen Creile, R. S. Sappington and L. McFarland. The mill is a total loss.

THE ABERDEEN MURDER.

The Murderers Make a Full Confession and Plead Guilty.

Special to the Appeal.]

ABERDEEN, Miss, December 27.—A fire broke out in Mr. J. F. Patterson's store last night. The damage was only about $500, which is fully covered by insurance.

THEY CONFESS.

W. Robert Jones, and the negro William Miller, murderers of the Walker brothers, have made full confessions, and on arraignment in the committing court to-day, on being asked if guilty or not guilty, each replied: "I am guilty." They were remanded to jail without bail. Judge Green has ordered a special term of court, to begin on the 30th of January, for their trial. Jones and Miller will have a speedy trial and early hanging.

THE HONOR HORROR.
The murderers of the Walker brothers, near Aberdeen, on the night of the 26th of November last (one white man and one negro), have, through the perseverance of Officers Sykes, Stout and Bean, been arrested, and are now lodged in jail. A special term of the Circuit Court has been ordered by Judge Green to convene on the 30th inst., for the purpose of giving the murderers a formal trial. This, of course, is right and much better than Lynch law. From the confessions hereto appended, made before Justice Sims, and which we copy from the Examiner, there is no room to doubt the guilt of the parties, and we presume there will be a tight rope performance near the banks of the 'Bigbee soon.

CONFESSION OF W. R. JONES (white)

I left home on the day the Walkers were at Alex Gilden's shop, in Tuskaloosa county, Ala., intending to go to the shop and collect some money, $5, from Bud Gilden, and then go on the railroad at Columbus or somewhere else, and if it did not cost me too much to go by train to Water Valley; if it cost much to walk through. I have a brother in law over there, Mr. Jack Boothe; thought of arranging to live out there and get a wagon and return for my family. When I reached the shop I found the Walkers; they invited me to go along with them and help trade off the old mule; I was glad to get to go along and joined them; we traveled on together until we reached Aberdeen; I had never thought of murdering or robbing them up to this time; the day of the murder I remained in town until about night; the wagons went out and struck camp; I followed on; I did not see William Miller in town and never saw him before; after we all went to bed, the Walker boys on a bed together and I on some sacks on the opposite side of the fire, I went to sleep, woke up in the night, supposed about midnight—(2 or three hours); got up and made up the fire and lay down again, but didn't go to sleep any more; this is the time I first conceived the idea of robbing the Walker brothers—I heard a noise out about the road; got up and walked over towards the real, saw this negro man, William Miller, called him to me and spoke to him. william-miller-aberdeen-1881-12-23.A16:
THEY WILL HANG.
The Murderers of the Walker Brothers Sentenced to Death.
Special to the Appeal.;
ABERDEEN, Miss., January 30.—A special term of court convened to-day, with Judge Green presiding and with Mr. Finley representing the State, for the purpose of trying W. Robert Jones, white, and William Miller, colored, charged with the murder of the three sons of Judge J. P. Walker, on the 26th of November, near this place. Jones plead guilty. Miller, who pleaded not guilty, was tried by a jury and convicted after but a few minutes delay, as the testimony was conclusive. Miller having previously made a full written confession, that was corroborated by the evidence. Sentence was passed upon both to be hung on the 3d of March. The trial was exceedingly quiet.
william-miller-aberdeen-1881-12-23.A17:
Mississippi Murderers Condemned to be Hanged.
MERIDIAN, Miss., January 30.—The trial of Bob C. Jones (white) and Billy Muller (colored) for the murder of the three sons of Judge J. P. Walker, of Alabama, took place to-day at Aberdeen. Jones pleaded guilty and Miller not guilty. Both were found guilty, and were sentenced to be hanged on March 3d.

william-nicholson-saunders-station-1881-.A2:
Exit "Butch" and "Frenchy."
Denver, Oct. 7.—The Republican's special says: Two robbers, known as Clark, alias "Butch" and "Frenchy," both formerly of the notorious Stockton gang, were lynched last night at Socorro, N. M. A week ago they robbed Brown & Manzanarie's commission house, at Lamy.

William Nicholson was also lynched at Saunders station, N. M., for murder.

Rain is falling copiously in New Mexico.
william-nicholson-saunders-station-1881-.A6:
LYNCH LAW IN NEW MEXICO.
CHICAGO, Oct. 8.—A dispatch from Las Vegas, New Mexico, says: "Two of the four men who robbed the store of Brown & Manzanares, at Laney Junction, recently, were arrested at Socorro on Wednesday, and yesterday morning were found hanging from the limb of a cottonwood tree on Methodist-ave., at that place, with a placard inscribed: 'The fate of footpads and horse thieves.' William Nicholson was lynched at Saunders' Station, N. M., for murder.
william-nicholson-saunders-station-1881-.A7:
NEW MEXICO.
Three Men Lynched - Shot in a Drunken Brawl.
SANTA FE, Oct. 8.—At Socorro on Thursday night, Clark, alias "Butch," and Wenchy, two notorious robbers, were hanged by a Vigilance Committee. At Saunders Station, on the Southern Pacific, Wm, Nicholson was lynched the same night for killing a man without provocation.
James Little was shot and killed yesterday at Los Vegas in a drunken row.
william-nicholson-saunders-station-1881-.A15:
Desperadoes Lynched.

A week ago they robbed Brown & Manzaro's commission house at Lamy. William Nicholson was lynched at Staurden's Station, New Mexico, for murder.
william-nicholson-saunders-station-1881-.A18: Concord Sun: Morton's girl house, at Big Lick, Stanly county, was destroyed by fire on Friday morning, 21st ult., about 5 oclock. A large quantity of cotton was burned with it, and the entire loss is about $1,000. Circumstances lead to the belief that it was an incendiary fire. We recently gave the rumor that William Nicholson, a refugee from this county, had been killed out West. The San Francisco Examiner, contains this item; "William Nicholson was lynched by a mob, for murder, at Sander's Station, New Mexico."
